Surah al-Mursalat (The Emissaries)
It has fifty verses and is Meccan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those sent forth in succession,﴾ ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing,﴾ ﴿by those that spread widely,﴾ ﴿by those that separate decisively,﴾ ﴿by those that deliver a reminder,﴾ ﴿as an excuse or a warning.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those sent forth in succession,﴾ ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing,﴾ ﴿by those that spread widely,﴾ ﴿by those that separate decisively,﴾ ﴿by those that deliver a reminder,﴾ ﴿as an excuse or a warning﴾. In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that these five words either refer to one single category or to several different categories.

As for the first possibility, they have mentioned several views on it.

The first: all of them refer to the angels. So "those sent forth" are the angels whom God sent, either to deliver blessing to some people or to deliver punishment to others.

As for His saying ﴿'urfan (in succession)﴾, it has several meanings:
One of them: successive, like the hair of the mane (ʿurf), as it is said: "They came as one mane," and "they gathered against him like the mane of the hyena" when they massed together against him.
The second: that it means ʿurf (customary goodness), which is the opposite of denial (nukra). For if these angels were sent for mercy, this meaning is evident in them; and if they were sent for punishment, that punishment, although it may not be known to the disbelievers, is known to the prophets and believers for whom God took vengeance upon them.
The third: that it is a verbal noun, as if it were said: "by those sent forth with sending," meaning in succession. The accusative of ﴿'urfan﴾ according to the first meaning is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); according to the second, it is an object, meaning: they were sent for goodness and customary kindness.

As for His saying ﴿fa-l-ʿāṣifāti ʿaṣfan (and by those that blow with violent blowing)﴾, it has two meanings:
The first: that when God the Exalted sent those angels, they swept through in their flight just as winds sweep.
The second: that these angels sweep away the soul of the disbeliever. It is said: "he swept away the thing" when he destroyed it and annihilated it. It is said: "a she-camel that sweeps (ʿaṣūd)," meaning she sweeps her rider away and passes on as if she were a wind in speed; and "war swept the people away," meaning it carried them off. The poet said:

*In a host, white and massed, it sweeps away the one who advances and the one who retreats.*

[Page 234]

As for His exalted saying ﴿wa-n-nāshirāti nashran (and by those that spread widely)﴾, its meaning is that they spread their wings when they descend to the earth; or they spread the laws upon the earth; or they spread mercy or punishment; or the intended meaning is the angels who spread the books on the Day of Reckoning, which are the books containing the deeds of the children of Adam. God the Exalted said: ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find spread open﴾ [al-Isra: 13]. In sum, they have spread the thing they were commanded to deliver to the people of the earth and to spread among them.

As for His exalted saying ﴿fa-l-fāriqāti farqan (and by those that separate decisively)﴾, its meaning is that they distinguish between truth and falsehood.

As for His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾, its meaning is that they deliver the reminder to the prophets. Then the meaning of "reminder" may be the general knowledge and wisdom, as He said: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Nahl: 2]. It may also be that the intended meaning is the Qur'an specifically, as in His saying: ﴿Has the reminder been cast upon him from among us?﴾ [al-Qamar: 25], and His saying: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be cast to you﴾ [al-Qasas: 86]. And although this one who casts it is Jibril alone, peace be upon him, it is permissible to refer to one by the name of a group as a form of honour.

Know that you have already understood that the purpose of an oath is to draw attention to the greatness of what is sworn by. The nobility of the angels and the loftiness of their rank is evident from several aspects:

One of them: the intensity of their constancy in obeying God the Exalted, as He said: ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾, and ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya: 27].

The second: they are of various categories. Among them are those sent to bring down revelation to the prophets; among them are those sent to accompany the children of Adam to record their deeds, a group by day and a group by night; among them are those sent to seize the souls of the children of Adam; among them are those who convey revelation from one heaven to another until the angel of that heaven brings the revelation down to the earth; and among them are the angels who descend every day from the Bayt al-Ma'mur to the Ka'ba, as has been reported in the traditions. All of this is included in His saying: ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾. Then there is the swiftness of their movement and their crossing of great distances in a short time, as in His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]. Then there is the spreading of their great wings when they fly, and the spreading of knowledge, wisdom, prophethood, guidance, direction, revelation and sending down, and the manifestation of the distinction between truth and falsehood through the sending down of that revelation, and the casting of the reminder into the heart and tongue through that revelation. In sum, the angels are the intermediaries between God the Exalted and His servants in attaining all worldly and otherworldly felicities, and both bodily and spiritual goods. Therefore God swore by them.

The second view: the intended meaning of all these five words is the winds. God swore by winds of punishment which He sent "in succession," meaning successive like the hair of the mane, as He said: ﴿He sends the winds﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], and ﴿And We sent the winds﴾ [al-Hijr: 22]. Then they grow strong until they become violent storms, and winds of mercy, which spread the clouds across the sky, as He said: ﴿And He it is who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], and He said: ﴿God is the One who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and He spreads them across the sky﴾ [al-Rum: 48]. It is also permissible to say that the winds assist plants, crops and trees in growth and sprouting, because they fertilise them, and thereby the plants emerge. This is as He said: ﴿And We sent the fertilising winds﴾ [al-Hijr: 22]. In this way the winds are spreaders of plant life. As for the winds being separators, there are several aspects:

One of them: the winds separate some parts of the clouds from others.

The second: God the Exalted destroyed some towns by sending winds upon them, as He said: ﴿As for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a violent screaming wind﴾ [al-Haqqa: 6], and that is a cause for the manifestation of the distinction between the friends of God and His enemies.

The third: when various winds arise and wondrous effects follow from them, such as the surging of clouds and the ruin of dwellings, people become compelled to return to God

[Page 235]

and to humble themselves at the door of His mercy. Thus a distinction arises between the one who affirms and the one who denies, and between the monotheist and the heretic. As for His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾, its meaning is that when a rational person witnesses the blowing of winds that uproot tents, demolish rocks and mountains, and raise waves, he holds fast to the remembrance of God and takes refuge in the help of God. So those winds become as if they had cast the remembrance, faith and servitude into the heart. There is no doubt that this attribution is figurative, since the remembrance came about at the occurrence of these winds.

The third view: some people have taken some of these five words to refer to the Qur'an, and in my opinion it is possible to take all of them as referring to the Qur'an. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth﴾ means the consecutive verses sent down through Jibril, peace be upon him, to Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying ﴿in succession﴾ means that these verses came down with every kind of customary goodness and benefit, and how could they not, since they guide to the path of salvation and lead to the gathering of all good. ﴿By those that blow with violent blowing﴾ means that the state of Islam and the Qur'an was weak at first, then it grew great and overcame all other religions, communities and creeds. It is as if the state of the Qur'an swept away all other states, communities and creeds, overpowered them, and made them false and void. His saying ﴿by those that spread widely﴾ means that the verses of the Qur'an spread the effects of wisdom and guidance into the hearts of the worlds, east and west. His saying ﴿by those that separate decisively﴾ is evident, because the verses of the Qur'an are what distinguish truth from falsehood, and for this reason God the Exalted named the Qur'an "the Criterion" (al-furqan). His saying ﴿by those that deliver a reminder﴾ is also clear, because the Qur'an is a reminder, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Ṣād. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾, ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾, and "admonition" (tadhkira), as He said: ﴿And indeed it is an admonition for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Haqqa: 48], and "remembrance" (dhikra), as He said: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder for the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. It thus becomes clear that these five words can be interpreted as referring to the Qur'an. Although no one has mentioned this, it is still a possibility.

The fourth view: these words may also be taken to refer to the sending of the prophets, peace be upon them all. ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾ are the persons who were sent with revelation containing every good and customary goodness, for there is no doubt that they were sent with "There is no god but God," which is the key to all good and customary goodness. ﴿By those that blow with violent blowing﴾ means that the affair of each messenger is at first small and weak, then it grows, becomes great, and gains strength like the blowing of winds. ﴿By those that spread widely﴾ means the spreading of their religion, their way and their doctrine. ﴿By those that separate decisively﴾ means that they distinguish between truth and falsehood, monotheism and atheism. ﴿By those that deliver a reminder﴾ means that they call creation to the remembrance of God, command them to it, and urge them towards it.

The fifth view: the intended meaning is that a man may be occupied with the interests of this world, absorbed in seeking its pleasures and comforts. In the midst of that, there arises in his heart a call to turn away from this world and to desire the service of his Master. These callings are "those sent forth in succession." These sent callings have two effects:

One of them: the removal of love for anything other than God the Exalted from the heart. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾.

The second: the effect of that call becomes manifest in all the limbs and organs, so that he hears only God, sees only God, and looks only to God. This is His saying ﴿by those that spread widely﴾. Then at that point the light of God's majesty is unveiled to him, so he sees Him as existent and sees everything else as non-existent. This is His saying ﴿by those that separate decisively﴾. Then the servant becomes like one who is famed for his love, and nothing remains in his heart or on his tongue except the remembrance of Him. This is His saying ﴿by those that deliver a reminder﴾.

Know that these last three aspects, although they have not been mentioned, are very much possible.

As for the second possibility, which is that the five words do not refer to one single thing, there are several views:

The first: what al-Zajjaj mentioned and what al-Qadi chose, namely that the first three are winds. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ refers to the winds that come in the customary manner, "those that blow with violent blowing" refers to the winds that intensify from it, and "those that spread widely" refers to the winds that spread the clouds.

[Page 236]

As for His saying ﴿fa-l-fāriqāti farqan (and by those that separate decisively)﴾, these are the angels who distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful, through what they bear of the Qur'an and revelation. Likewise His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾ refers to the angels who bear the reminder and deliver it to the messengers.

If it is said: what is the affinity between the winds and the angels that would justify combining them in the oath?

We reply: the angels are spiritual beings, and because of their subtlety and the swiftness of their movements, they are like the winds.

The second view: the first two are the winds. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ and ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾ refer to the winds, and the remaining three are the angels, because they spread the revelation and religion. Then this revelation has two effects:

One of them: the occurrence of a distinction between the one who is right and the one who is wrong.

The second: the manifestation of the remembrance of God in the hearts and on the tongues.

I have not seen this view attributed to anyone, but it is also clearly possible. What confirms it is that He said: ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ and ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾, connecting the second to the first with the particle fa (then). Then He mentioned the particle wa (and) and said ﴿by those that spread widely﴾, and connected the remaining two to it with the particle fa. This indicates that the first two are distinct from the last three.

Third opinion: it may be said that the first two oaths refer to the angels. So ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ refers to the angels of mercy, and ﴿by those that blow violently﴾ refers to the angels of punishment. The remaining three refer to the verses of the Qur'an, because they spread the truth into hearts and souls, distinguish between truth and falsehood, and place the remembrance (dhikr) on hearts and tongues. I have not seen this opinion attributed to anyone, and it is a possibility. Whoever considers what we have mentioned can derive several other interpretations from it. And God knows best.

Second issue: al-Qaffal said: The reason for the fa' (فاء, "then/so") appearing with some of the things sworn by, and the waw (واو, "and") with others, is based on the principle that, according to the linguists, the fa' implies connection and dependency. When it is said, "Zayd stood up and then (fa) left," the meaning is that he stood up in order to leave, so his standing was the cause of his leaving and connected to it. When it is said, "Zayd stood up and (wa) left," these are two separate reports, each standing on its own and not dependent on the other. Having laid down this principle, al-Qaffal then derived from it, in this verse, explanations that my heart does not lean towards. I will derive from this principle and say: as for whoever takes the first two as attributes of one thing and the last three as attributes of another thing, the difficulty disappears. As for whoever takes all of them as attributes of one thing: if we apply them to the angels, then when the angels are sent they fly swiftly, and that flight is the blowing violently ('asf). So the blowing is consequent upon the sending, and therefore the fa' is used. As for the spreading (nashr), it is not consequent upon the sending, because when the angels first convey the revelation to the messengers, that religion does not immediately become famous and widespread; rather, the people harm the prophets at first and attribute to them lying, sorcery and madness. Therefore the fa', which denotes immediate sequence, is not used, but the waw is used. Furthermore, once the spreading occurs, the distinction between truth and falsehood and the prominence of the mention of the truth on tongues result from it, so these two matters are introduced with the fa'. It is as if, and God knows best, it was said: "O Muhammad, I have sent the angel to you with the revelation, which is the sign of every happiness and the opening of every good. But do not expect that we will spread that matter immediately; rather, patience and bearing hardship are necessary. Then, when the time of victory comes, I will make your religion manifest and widespread in the east and west of the world. At that time of spreading the distinction will become evident, so the false religions will become weak and fallen, and your religion, the true religion, will be manifest and dominant. Then God will make that remembrance manifest on tongues, in the prayer niches (mihrab) and on the pulpits, and the world will become filled with the remembrance of God." This is what we get if we apply these five expressions to the angels. Whoever understands this approach can mention what is similar to it concerning the winds and other interpretations. And God knows best.

As for His saying ﴿excuses or warnings﴾ (عُذْرًا أوْ نُذْرًا), there are two issues concerning it:

Page 237

First issue: There are two readings for these two words. The first is with light pronunciation (تخفيف), which is the reading of Abu 'Amr and Asim through the transmission of Hafs. The rest read with heavy pronunciation (تثقيل). As for the light pronunciation, there is no dispute that it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "giving excuse" (i'dhar) and "giving warning" (indhar). As for the heavy pronunciation, Abu 'Ubayda claimed that it is a plural and not a verbal noun. Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj claimed that it is a verbal noun. The heavy and light forms are two dialects. Abu 'Ali affirmed the view of al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj and said: "al-'udhr (عُذُر), al-'adhir (عَذِير), al-nudhr (نُذُر) and al-nadhir (نَذِير) are like nukr and nakir." Then Abu 'Ali said: "In the reading of the one who uses the heavy form, it is also permissible that ʿudhran (عُذُرًا) is the plural of ʿadhir (عاذِر), like sharuf and sharif, and likewise nudhur may be the plural of nadhir." God Most High said: ﴿This is a warner from the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56].

Second issue: There are three possible grammatical analyses of the accusative case (نصب). If it is a verbal noun, there are two:
The first: it is an object in apposition (بدل) to His saying "dhikran" (ذِكْرًا).
The second: it is an object of purpose (مفعول له), and the meaning is: "and those who cast the remembrance as excuse or warning."
If it is a plural, it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (حال) of the casting (الإلقاء), and the meaning is: "those who cast the remembrance while being excusers and warners."

In the midst of that, there arises in his heart a call to turn away from this world and to desire the service of his Master. These callings are "those sent forth in succession." These sent callings have two effects:

One of them: the removal of love for anything other than God the Exalted from the heart. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾.

The second: the effect of that call becomes manifest in all the limbs and organs, so that he hears only God, sees only God, and looks only to God. This is His saying ﴿by those that spread widely﴾. Then at that point the light of God's majesty is unveiled to him, so he sees Him as existent and sees everything else as non-existent. This is His saying ﴿by those that separate decisively﴾. Then the servant becomes like one who is famed for his love, and nothing remains in his heart or on his tongue except the remembrance of Him. This is His saying ﴿by those that deliver a reminder﴾.

Know that these last three aspects, although they have not been mentioned, are very much possible.

As for the second possibility, which is that the five words do not refer to one single thing, there are several views:

The first: what al-Zajjaj mentioned and what al-Qadi chose, namely that the first three are winds. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ refers to the winds that come in the customary manner, "those that blow with violent blowing" refers to the winds that intensify from it, and "those that spread widely" refers to the winds that spread the clouds.

[Page 236]

As for His saying ﴿fa-l-fāriqāti farqan (and by those that separate decisively)﴾, these are the angels who distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful, through what they bear of the Qur'an and revelation. Likewise His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾ refers to the angels who bear the reminder and deliver it to the messengers.

If it is said: what is the affinity between the winds and the angels that would justify combining them in the oath?

We reply: the angels are spiritual beings, and because of their subtlety and the swiftness of their movements, they are like the winds.

The second view: the first two are the winds. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ and ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾ refer to the winds, and the remaining three are the angels, because they spread the revelation and religion. Then this revelation has two effects:

One of them: the occurrence of a distinction between the one who is right and the one who is wrong.

The second: the manifestation of the remembrance of God in the hearts and on the tongues.

I have not seen this view attributed to anyone, but it is also clearly possible. What confirms it is that He said: ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ and ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾, connecting the second to the first with the particle fa (then). Then He mentioned the particle wa (and) and said ﴿by those that spread widely﴾, and connected the remaining two to it with the particle fa. This indicates that the first two are distinct from the last three.

Third opinion: it may be said that the first two oaths refer to the angels. So ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ refers to the angels of mercy, and ﴿by those that blow violently﴾ refers to the angels of punishment. The remaining three refer to the verses of the Qur'an, because they spread the truth into hearts and souls, distinguish between truth and falsehood, and place the remembrance (dhikr) on hearts and tongues. I have not seen this opinion attributed to anyone, and it is a possibility. Whoever considers what we have mentioned can derive several other interpretations from it. And God knows best.

Second issue: al-Qaffal said: The reason for the fa' (فاء, "then/so") appearing with some of the things sworn by, and the waw (واو, "and") with others, is based on the principle that, according to the linguists, the fa' implies connection and dependency. When it is said, "Zayd stood up and then (fa) left," the meaning is that he stood up in order to leave, so his standing was the cause of his leaving and connected to it. When it is said, "Zayd stood up and (wa) left," these are two separate reports, each standing on its own and not dependent on the other. Having laid down this principle, al-Qaffal then derived from it, in this verse, explanations that my heart does not lean towards. I will derive from this principle and say: as for whoever takes the first two as attributes of one thing and the last three as attributes of another thing, the difficulty disappears. As for whoever takes all of them as attributes of one thing: if we apply them to the angels, then when the angels are sent they fly swiftly, and that flight is the blowing violently ('asf). So the blowing is consequent upon the sending, and therefore the fa' is used. As for the spreading (nashr), it is not consequent upon the sending, because when the angels first convey the revelation to the messengers, that religion does not immediately become famous and widespread; rather, the people harm the prophets at first and attribute to them lying, sorcery and madness. Therefore the fa', which denotes immediate sequence, is not used, but the waw is used. Furthermore, once the spreading occurs, the distinction between truth and falsehood and the prominence of the mention of the truth on tongues result from it, so these two matters are introduced with the fa'. It is as if, and God knows best, it was said: "O Muhammad, I have sent the angel to you with the revelation, which is the sign of every happiness and the opening of every good. But do not expect that we will spread that matter immediately; rather, patience and bearing hardship are necessary. Then, when the time of victory comes, I will make your religion manifest and widespread in the east and west of the world. At that time of spreading the distinction will become evident, so the false religions will become weak and fallen, and your religion, the true religion, will be manifest and dominant. Then God will make that remembrance manifest on tongues, in the prayer niches (mihrab) and on the pulpits, and the world will become filled with the remembrance of God." This is what we get if we apply these five expressions to the angels. Whoever understands this approach can mention what is similar to it concerning the winds and other interpretations. And God knows best.

As for His saying ﴿excuses or warnings﴾ (عُذْرًا أوْ نُذْرًا), there are two issues concerning it:

Page 237

First issue: There are two readings for these two words. The first is with light pronunciation (تخفيف), which is the reading of Abu 'Amr and Asim through the transmission of Hafs. The rest read with heavy pronunciation (تثقيل). As for the light pronunciation, there is no dispute that it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "giving excuse" (i'dhar) and "giving warning" (indhar). As for the heavy pronunciation, Abu 'Ubayda claimed that it is a plural and not a verbal noun. Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj claimed that it is a verbal noun. The heavy and light forms are two dialects. Abu 'Ali affirmed the view of al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj and said: "al-'udhr (عُذُر), al-'adhir (عَذِير), al-nudhr (نُذُر) and al-nadhir (نَذِير) are like nukr and nakir." Then Abu 'Ali said: "In the reading of the one who uses the heavy form, it is also permissible that ʿudhran (عُذُرًا) is the plural of ʿadhir (عاذِر), like sharuf and sharif, and likewise nudhur may be the plural of nadhir." God Most High said: ﴿This is a warner from the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56].

Second issue: There are three possible grammatical analyses of the accusative case (نصب). If it is a verbal noun, there are two:
The first: it is an object in apposition (بدل) to His saying "dhikran" (ذِكْرًا).
The second: it is an object of purpose (مفعول له), and the meaning is: "and those who cast the remembrance as excuse or warning."
If it is a plural, it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (حال) of the casting (الإلقاء), and the meaning is: "those who cast the remembrance while being excusers and warners."

[Page 233]

Surah al-Mursalat (The Emissaries)
It has fifty verses and is Meccan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those sent forth in succession,﴾ ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing,﴾ ﴿by those that spread widely,﴾ ﴿by those that separate decisively,﴾ ﴿by those that deliver a reminder,﴾ ﴿as an excuse or a warning.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those sent forth in succession,﴾ ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing,﴾ ﴿by those that spread widely,﴾ ﴿by those that separate decisively,﴾ ﴿by those that deliver a reminder,﴾ ﴿as an excuse or a warning﴾. In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that these five words either refer to one single category or to several different categories.

As for the first possibility, they have mentioned several views on it.

The first: all of them refer to the angels. So "those sent forth" are the angels whom God sent, either to deliver blessing to some people or to deliver punishment to others.

As for His saying ﴿'urfan (in succession)﴾, it has several meanings:
One of them: successive, like the hair of the mane (ʿurf), as it is said: "They came as one mane," and "they gathered against him like the mane of the hyena" when they massed together against him.
The second: that it means ʿurf (customary goodness), which is the opposite of denial (nukra). For if these angels were sent for mercy, this meaning is evident in them; and if they were sent for punishment, that punishment, although it may not be known to the disbelievers, is known to the prophets and believers for whom God took vengeance upon them.
The third: that it is a verbal noun, as if it were said: "by those sent forth with sending," meaning in succession. The accusative of ﴿'urfan﴾ according to the first meaning is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); according to the second, it is an object, meaning: they were sent for goodness and customary kindness.

As for His saying ﴿fa-l-ʿāṣifāti ʿaṣfan (and by those that blow with violent blowing)﴾, it has two meanings:
The first: that when God the Exalted sent those angels, they swept through in their flight just as winds sweep.
The second: that these angels sweep away the soul of the disbeliever. It is said: "he swept away the thing" when he destroyed it and annihilated it. It is said: "a she-camel that sweeps (ʿaṣūd)," meaning she sweeps her rider away and passes on as if she were a wind in speed; and "war swept the people away," meaning it carried them off. The poet said:

*In a host, white and massed, it sweeps away the one who advances and the one who retreats.*

[Page 234]

As for His exalted saying ﴿wa-n-nāshirāti nashran (and by those that spread widely)﴾, its meaning is that they spread their wings when they descend to the earth; or they spread the laws upon the earth; or they spread mercy or punishment; or the intended meaning is the angels who spread the books on the Day of Reckoning, which are the books containing the deeds of the children of Adam. God the Exalted said: ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find spread open﴾ [al-Isra: 13]. In sum, they have spread the thing they were commanded to deliver to the people of the earth and to spread among them.

As for His exalted saying ﴿fa-l-fāriqāti farqan (and by those that separate decisively)﴾, its meaning is that they distinguish between truth and falsehood.

As for His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾, its meaning is that they deliver the reminder to the prophets. Then the meaning of "reminder" may be the general knowledge and wisdom, as He said: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Nahl: 2]. It may also be that the intended meaning is the Qur'an specifically, as in His saying: ﴿Has the reminder been cast upon him from among us?﴾ [al-Qamar: 25], and His saying: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be cast to you﴾ [al-Qasas: 86]. And although this one who casts it is Jibril alone, peace be upon him, it is permissible to refer to one by the name of a group as a form of honour.

Know that you have already understood that the purpose of an oath is to draw attention to the greatness of what is sworn by. The nobility of the angels and the loftiness of their rank is evident from several aspects:

One of them: the intensity of their constancy in obeying God the Exalted, as He said: ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾, and ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya: 27].

The second: they are of various categories. Among them are those sent to bring down revelation to the prophets; among them are those sent to accompany the children of Adam to record their deeds, a group by day and a group by night; among them are those sent to seize the souls of the children of Adam; among them are those who convey revelation from one heaven to another until the angel of that heaven brings the revelation down to the earth; and among them are the angels who descend every day from the Bayt al-Ma'mur to the Ka'ba, as has been reported in the traditions. All of this is included in His saying: ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾. Then there is the swiftness of their movement and their crossing of great distances in a short time, as in His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]. Then there is the spreading of their great wings when they fly, and the spreading of knowledge, wisdom, prophethood, guidance, direction, revelation and sending down, and the manifestation of the distinction between truth and falsehood through the sending down of that revelation, and the casting of the reminder into the heart and tongue through that revelation. In sum, the angels are the intermediaries between God the Exalted and His servants in attaining all worldly and otherworldly felicities, and both bodily and spiritual goods. Therefore God swore by them.

The second view: the intended meaning of all these five words is the winds. God swore by winds of punishment which He sent "in succession," meaning successive like the hair of the mane, as He said: ﴿He sends the winds﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], and ﴿And We sent the winds﴾ [al-Hijr: 22]. Then they grow strong until they become violent storms, and winds of mercy, which spread the clouds across the sky, as He said: ﴿And He it is who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], and He said: ﴿God is the One who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and He spreads them across the sky﴾ [al-Rum: 48]. It is also permissible to say that the winds assist plants, crops and trees in growth and sprouting, because they fertilise them, and thereby the plants emerge. This is as He said: ﴿And We sent the fertilising winds﴾ [al-Hijr: 22]. In this way the winds are spreaders of plant life. As for the winds being separators, there are several aspects:

One of them: the winds separate some parts of the clouds from others.

The second: God the Exalted destroyed some towns by sending winds upon them, as He said: ﴿As for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a violent screaming wind﴾ [al-Haqqa: 6], and that is a cause for the manifestation of the distinction between the friends of God and His enemies.

The third: when various winds arise and wondrous effects follow from them, such as the surging of clouds and the ruin of dwellings, people become compelled to return to God

[Page 235]

and to humble themselves at the door of His mercy. Thus a distinction arises between the one who affirms and the one who denies, and between the monotheist and the heretic. As for His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾, its meaning is that when a rational person witnesses the blowing of winds that uproot tents, demolish rocks and mountains, and raise waves, he holds fast to the remembrance of God and takes refuge in the help of God. So those winds become as if they had cast the remembrance, faith and servitude into the heart. There is no doubt that this attribution is figurative, since the remembrance came about at the occurrence of these winds.

The third view: some people have taken some of these five words to refer to the Qur'an, and in my opinion it is possible to take all of them as referring to the Qur'an. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth﴾ means the consecutive verses sent down through Jibril, peace be upon him, to Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying ﴿in succession﴾ means that these verses came down with every kind of customary goodness and benefit, and how could they not, since they guide to the path of salvation and lead to the gathering of all good. ﴿By those that blow with violent blowing﴾ means that the state of Islam and the Qur'an was weak at first, then it grew great and overcame all other religions, communities and creeds. It is as if the state of the Qur'an swept away all other states, communities and creeds, overpowered them, and made them false and void. His saying ﴿by those that spread widely﴾ means that the verses of the Qur'an spread the effects of wisdom and guidance into the hearts of the worlds, east and west. His saying ﴿by those that separate decisively﴾ is evident, because the verses of the Qur'an are what distinguish truth from falsehood, and for this reason God the Exalted named the Qur'an "the Criterion" (al-furqan). His saying ﴿by those that deliver a reminder﴾ is also clear, because the Qur'an is a reminder, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Ṣād. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾, ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾, and "admonition" (tadhkira), as He said: ﴿And indeed it is an admonition for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Haqqa: 48], and "remembrance" (dhikra), as He said: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder for the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. It thus becomes clear that these five words can be interpreted as referring to the Qur'an. Although no one has mentioned this, it is still a possibility.

The second: that these angels sweep away the soul of the disbeliever. It is said: "he swept away the thing" when he destroyed it and annihilated it. It is said: "a she-camel that sweeps (ʿaṣūd)," meaning she sweeps her rider away and passes on as if she were a wind in speed; and "war swept the people away," meaning it carried them off. The poet said:

*In a host, white and massed, it sweeps away the one who advances and the one who retreats.*

[Page 234]

As for His exalted saying ﴿wa-n-nāshirāti nashran (and by those that spread widely)﴾, its meaning is that they spread their wings when they descend to the earth; or they spread the laws upon the earth; or they spread mercy or punishment; or the intended meaning is the angels who spread the books on the Day of Reckoning, which are the books containing the deeds of the children of Adam. God the Exalted said: ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find spread open﴾ [al-Isra: 13]. In sum, they have spread the thing they were commanded to deliver to the people of the earth and to spread among them.

As for His exalted saying ﴿fa-l-fāriqāti farqan (and by those that separate decisively)﴾, its meaning is that they distinguish between truth and falsehood.

As for His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾, its meaning is that they deliver the reminder to the prophets. Then the meaning of "reminder" may be the general knowledge and wisdom, as He said: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Nahl: 2]. It may also be that the intended meaning is the Qur'an specifically, as in His saying: ﴿Has the reminder been cast upon him from among us?﴾ [al-Qamar: 25], and His saying: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be cast to you﴾ [al-Qasas: 86]. And although this one who casts it is Jibril alone, peace be upon him, it is permissible to refer to one by the name of a group as a form of honour.

Know that you have already understood that the purpose of an oath is to draw attention to the greatness of what is sworn by. The nobility of the angels and the loftiness of their rank is evident from several aspects:

One of them: the intensity of their constancy in obeying God the Exalted, as He said: ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾, and ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya: 27].

The second: they are of various categories. Among them are those sent to bring down revelation to the prophets; among them are those sent to accompany the children of Adam to record their deeds, a group by day and a group by night; among them are those sent to seize the souls of the children of Adam; among them are those who convey revelation from one heaven to another until the angel of that heaven brings the revelation down to the earth; and among them are the angels who descend every day from the Bayt al-Ma'mur to the Ka'ba, as has been reported in the traditions. All of this is included in His saying: ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾. Then there is the swiftness of their movement and their crossing of great distances in a short time, as in His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]. Then there is the spreading of their great wings when they fly, and the spreading of knowledge, wisdom, prophethood, guidance, direction, revelation and sending down, and the manifestation of the distinction between truth and falsehood through the sending down of that revelation, and the casting of the reminder into the heart and tongue through that revelation. In sum, the angels are the intermediaries between God the Exalted and His servants in attaining all worldly and otherworldly felicities, and both bodily and spiritual goods. Therefore God swore by them.

The second view: the intended meaning of all these five words is the winds. God swore by winds of punishment which He sent "in succession," meaning successive like the hair of the mane, as He said: ﴿He sends the winds﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], and ﴿And We sent the winds﴾ [al-Hijr: 22]. Then they grow strong until they become violent storms, and winds of mercy, which spread the clouds across the sky, as He said: ﴿And He it is who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], and He said: ﴿God is the One who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and He spreads them across the sky﴾ [al-Rum: 48]. It is also permissible to say that the winds assist plants, crops and trees in growth and sprouting, because they fertilise them, and thereby the plants emerge. This is as He said: ﴿And We sent the fertilising winds﴾ [al-Hijr: 22]. In this way the winds are spreaders of plant life. As for the winds being separators, there are several aspects:

One of them: the winds separate some parts of the clouds from others.

The second: God the Exalted destroyed some towns by sending winds upon them, as He said: ﴿As for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a violent screaming wind﴾ [al-Haqqa: 6], and that is a cause for the manifestation of the distinction between the friends of God and His enemies.

The third: when various winds arise and wondrous effects follow from them, such as the surging of clouds and the ruin of dwellings, people become compelled to return to God

[Page 235]

and to humble themselves at the door of His mercy. Thus a distinction arises between the one who affirms and the one who denies, and between the monotheist and the heretic. As for His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾, its meaning is that when a rational person witnesses the blowing of winds that uproot tents, demolish rocks and mountains, and raise waves, he holds fast to the remembrance of God and takes refuge in the help of God. So those winds become as if they had cast the remembrance, faith and servitude into the heart. There is no doubt that this attribution is figurative, since the remembrance came about at the occurrence of these winds.

The third view: some people have taken some of these five words to refer to the Qur'an, and in my opinion it is possible to take all of them as referring to the Qur'an. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth﴾ means the consecutive verses sent down through Jibril, peace be upon him, to Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying ﴿in succession﴾ means that these verses came down with every kind of customary goodness and benefit, and how could they not, since they guide to the path of salvation and lead to the gathering of all good. ﴿By those that blow with violent blowing﴾ means that the state of Islam and the Qur'an was weak at first, then it grew great and overcame all other religions, communities and creeds. It is as if the state of the Qur'an swept away all other states, communities and creeds, overpowered them, and made them false and void. His saying ﴿by those that spread widely﴾ means that the verses of the Qur'an spread the effects of wisdom and guidance into the hearts of the worlds, east and west. His saying ﴿by those that separate decisively﴾ is evident, because the verses of the Qur'an are what distinguish truth from falsehood, and for this reason God the Exalted named the Qur'an "the Criterion" (al-furqan). His saying ﴿by those that deliver a reminder﴾ is also clear, because the Qur'an is a reminder, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Ṣād. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾, ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾, and "admonition" (tadhkira), as He said: ﴿And indeed it is an admonition for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Haqqa: 48], and "remembrance" (dhikra), as He said: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder for the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. It thus becomes clear that these five words can be interpreted as referring to the Qur'an. Although no one has mentioned this, it is still a possibility.

The fourth view: these words may also be taken to refer to the sending of the prophets, peace be upon them all. ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾ are the persons who were sent with revelation containing every good and customary goodness, for there is no doubt that they were sent with "There is no god but God," which is the key to all good and customary goodness. ﴿By those that blow with violent blowing﴾ means that the affair of each messenger is at first small and weak, then it grows, becomes great, and gains strength like the blowing of winds. ﴿By those that spread widely﴾ means the spreading of their religion, their way and their doctrine. ﴿By those that separate decisively﴾ means that they distinguish between truth and falsehood, monotheism and atheism. ﴿By those that deliver a reminder﴾ means that they call creation to the remembrance of God, command them to it, and urge them towards it.

The fifth view: the intended meaning is that a man may be occupied with the interests of this world, absorbed in seeking its pleasures and comforts. In the midst of that, there arises in his heart a call to turn away from this world and to desire the service of his Master. These callings are "those sent forth in succession." These sent callings have two effects:

One of them: the removal of love for anything other than God the Exalted from the heart. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾.

The second: the effect of that call becomes manifest in all the limbs and organs, so that he hears only God, sees only God, and looks only to God. This is His saying ﴿by those that spread widely﴾. Then at that point the light of God's majesty is unveiled to him, so he sees Him as existent and sees everything else as non-existent. This is His saying ﴿by those that separate decisively﴾. Then the servant becomes like one who is famed for his love, and nothing remains in his heart or on his tongue except the remembrance of Him. This is His saying ﴿by those that deliver a reminder﴾.

Know that these last three aspects, although they have not been mentioned, are very much possible.

As for the second possibility, which is that the five words do not refer to one single thing, there are several views:

The first: what al-Zajjaj mentioned and what al-Qadi chose, namely that the first three are winds. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ refers to the winds that come in the customary manner, "those that blow with violent blowing" refers to the winds that intensify from it, and "those that spread widely" refers to the winds that spread the clouds.

[Page 236]

As for His saying ﴿fa-l-fāriqāti farqan (and by those that separate decisively)﴾, these are the angels who distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful, through what they bear of the Qur'an and revelation. Likewise His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾ refers to the angels who bear the reminder and deliver it to the messengers.

If it is said: what is the affinity between the winds and the angels that would justify combining them in the oath?

We reply: the angels are spiritual beings, and because of their subtlety and the swiftness of their movements, they are like the winds.

The second view: the first two are the winds. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ and ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾ refer to the winds, and the remaining three are the angels, because they spread the revelation and religion. Then this revelation has two effects:

One of them: the occurrence of a distinction between the one who is right and the one who is wrong.

The second: the manifestation of the remembrance of God in the hearts and on the tongues.

I have not seen this view attributed to anyone, but it is also clearly possible. What confirms it is that He said: ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ and ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾, connecting the second to the first with the particle fa (then). Then He mentioned the particle wa (and) and said ﴿by those that spread widely﴾, and connected the remaining two to it with the particle fa. This indicates that the first two are distinct from the last three.

Third opinion: it may be said that the first two oaths refer to the angels. So ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ refers to the angels of mercy, and ﴿by those that blow violently﴾ refers to the angels of punishment. The remaining three refer to the verses of the Qur'an, because they spread the truth into hearts and souls, distinguish between truth and falsehood, and place the remembrance (dhikr) on hearts and tongues. I have not seen this opinion attributed to anyone, and it is a possibility. Whoever considers what we have mentioned can derive several other interpretations from it. And God knows best.

Second issue: al-Qaffal said: The reason for the fa' (فاء, "then/so") appearing with some of the things sworn by, and the waw (واو, "and") with others, is based on the principle that, according to the linguists, the fa' implies connection and dependency. When it is said, "Zayd stood up and then (fa) left," the meaning is that he stood up in order to leave, so his standing was the cause of his leaving and connected to it. When it is said, "Zayd stood up and (wa) left," these are two separate reports, each standing on its own and not dependent on the other. Having laid down this principle, al-Qaffal then derived from it, in this verse, explanations that my heart does not lean towards. I will derive from this principle and say: as for whoever takes the first two as attributes of one thing and the last three as attributes of another thing, the difficulty disappears. As for whoever takes all of them as attributes of one thing: if we apply them to the angels, then when the angels are sent they fly swiftly, and that flight is the blowing violently ('asf). So the blowing is consequent upon the sending, and therefore the fa' is used. As for the spreading (nashr), it is not consequent upon the sending, because when the angels first convey the revelation to the messengers, that religion does not immediately become famous and widespread; rather, the people harm the prophets at first and attribute to them lying, sorcery and madness. Therefore the fa', which denotes immediate sequence, is not used, but the waw is used. Furthermore, once the spreading occurs, the distinction between truth and falsehood and the prominence of the mention of the truth on tongues result from it, so these two matters are introduced with the fa'. It is as if, and God knows best, it was said: "O Muhammad, I have sent the angel to you with the revelation, which is the sign of every happiness and the opening of every good. But do not expect that we will spread that matter immediately; rather, patience and bearing hardship are necessary. Then, when the time of victory comes, I will make your religion manifest and widespread in the east and west of the world. At that time of spreading the distinction will become evident, so the false religions will become weak and fallen, and your religion, the true religion, will be manifest and dominant. Then God will make that remembrance manifest on tongues, in the prayer niches (mihrab) and on the pulpits, and the world will become filled with the remembrance of God." This is what we get if we apply these five expressions to the angels. Whoever understands this approach can mention what is similar to it concerning the winds and other interpretations. And God knows best.

As for His saying ﴿excuses or warnings﴾ (عُذْرًا أوْ نُذْرًا), there are two issues concerning it:

Page 237

First issue: There are two readings for these two words. The first is with light pronunciation (تخفيف), which is the reading of Abu 'Amr and Asim through the transmission of Hafs. The rest read with heavy pronunciation (تثقيل). As for the light pronunciation, there is no dispute that it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "giving excuse" (i'dhar) and "giving warning" (indhar). As for the heavy pronunciation, Abu 'Ubayda claimed that it is a plural and not a verbal noun. Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj claimed that it is a verbal noun. The heavy and light forms are two dialects. Abu 'Ali affirmed the view of al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj and said: "al-'udhr (عُذُر), al-'adhir (عَذِير), al-nudhr (نُذُر) and al-nadhir (نَذِير) are like nukr and nakir." Then Abu 'Ali said: "In the reading of the one who uses the heavy form, it is also permissible that ʿudhran (عُذُرًا) is the plural of ʿadhir (عاذِر), like sharuf and sharif, and likewise nudhur may be the plural of nadhir." God Most High said: ﴿This is a warner from the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56].

Second issue: There are three possible grammatical analyses of the accusative case (نصب). If it is a verbal noun, there are two:
The first: it is an object in apposition (بدل) to His saying "dhikran" (ذِكْرًا).
The second: it is an object of purpose (مفعول له), and the meaning is: "and those who cast the remembrance as excuse or warning."
If it is a plural, it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (حال) of the casting (الإلقاء), and the meaning is: "those who cast the remembrance while being excusers and warners."

The second view: the first two are the winds. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ and ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾ refer to the winds, and the remaining three are the angels, because they spread the revelation and religion. Then this revelation has two effects:

One of them: the occurrence of a distinction between the one who is right and the one who is wrong.

The second: the manifestation of the remembrance of God in the hearts and on the tongues.

I have not seen this view attributed to anyone, but it is also clearly possible. What confirms it is that He said: ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ and ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾, connecting the second to the first with the particle fa (then). Then He mentioned the particle wa (and) and said ﴿by those that spread widely﴾, and connected the remaining two to it with the particle fa. This indicates that the first two are distinct from the last three.

Third opinion: it may be said that the first two oaths refer to the angels. So ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ refers to the angels of mercy, and ﴿by those that blow violently﴾ refers to the angels of punishment. The remaining three refer to the verses of the Qur'an, because they spread the truth into hearts and souls, distinguish between truth and falsehood, and place the remembrance (dhikr) on hearts and tongues. I have not seen this opinion attributed to anyone, and it is a possibility. Whoever considers what we have mentioned can derive several other interpretations from it. And God knows best.

Second issue: al-Qaffal said: The reason for the fa' (فاء, "then/so") appearing with some of the things sworn by, and the waw (واو, "and") with others, is based on the principle that, according to the linguists, the fa' implies connection and dependency. When it is said, "Zayd stood up and then (fa) left," the meaning is that he stood up in order to leave, so his standing was the cause of his leaving and connected to it. When it is said, "Zayd stood up and (wa) left," these are two separate reports, each standing on its own and not dependent on the other. Having laid down this principle, al-Qaffal then derived from it, in this verse, explanations that my heart does not lean towards. I will derive from this principle and say: as for whoever takes the first two as attributes of one thing and the last three as attributes of another thing, the difficulty disappears. As for whoever takes all of them as attributes of one thing: if we apply them to the angels, then when the angels are sent they fly swiftly, and that flight is the blowing violently ('asf). So the blowing is consequent upon the sending, and therefore the fa' is used. As for the spreading (nashr), it is not consequent upon the sending, because when the angels first convey the revelation to the messengers, that religion does not immediately become famous and widespread; rather, the people harm the prophets at first and attribute to them lying, sorcery and madness. Therefore the fa', which denotes immediate sequence, is not used, but the waw is used. Furthermore, once the spreading occurs, the distinction between truth and falsehood and the prominence of the mention of the truth on tongues result from it, so these two matters are introduced with the fa'. It is as if, and God knows best, it was said: "O Muhammad, I have sent the angel to you with the revelation, which is the sign of every happiness and the opening of every good. But do not expect that we will spread that matter immediately; rather, patience and bearing hardship are necessary. Then, when the time of victory comes, I will make your religion manifest and widespread in the east and west of the world. At that time of spreading the distinction will become evident, so the false religions will become weak and fallen, and your religion, the true religion, will be manifest and dominant. Then God will make that remembrance manifest on tongues, in the prayer niches (mihrab) and on the pulpits, and the world will become filled with the remembrance of God." This is what we get if we apply these five expressions to the angels. Whoever understands this approach can mention what is similar to it concerning the winds and other interpretations. And God knows best.

As for His saying ﴿excuses or warnings﴾ (عُذْرًا أوْ نُذْرًا), there are two issues concerning it:

Page 237

First issue: There are two readings for these two words. The first is with light pronunciation (تخفيف), which is the reading of Abu 'Amr and Asim through the transmission of Hafs. The rest read with heavy pronunciation (تثقيل). As for the light pronunciation, there is no dispute that it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "giving excuse" (i'dhar) and "giving warning" (indhar). As for the heavy pronunciation, Abu 'Ubayda claimed that it is a plural and not a verbal noun. Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj claimed that it is a verbal noun. The heavy and light forms are two dialects. Abu 'Ali affirmed the view of al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj and said: "al-'udhr (عُذُر), al-'adhir (عَذِير), al-nudhr (نُذُر) and al-nadhir (نَذِير) are like nukr and nakir." Then Abu 'Ali said: "In the reading of the one who uses the heavy form, it is also permissible that ʿudhran (عُذُرًا) is the plural of ʿadhir (عاذِر), like sharuf and sharif, and likewise nudhur may be the plural of nadhir." God Most High said: ﴿This is a warner from the warners of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56].

Second issue: There are three possible grammatical analyses of the accusative case (نصب). If it is a verbal noun, there are two:
The first: it is an object in apposition (بدل) to His saying "dhikran" (ذِكْرًا).
The second: it is an object of purpose (مفعول له), and the meaning is: "and those who cast the remembrance as excuse or warning."
If it is a plural, it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (حال) of the casting (الإلقاء), and the meaning is: "those who cast the remembrance while being excusers and warners."

[Page 233]

Surah al-Mursalat (The Emissaries)
It has fifty verses and is Meccan.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those sent forth in succession,﴾ ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing,﴾ ﴿by those that spread widely,﴾ ﴿by those that separate decisively,﴾ ﴿by those that deliver a reminder,﴾ ﴿as an excuse or a warning.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By those sent forth in succession,﴾ ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing,﴾ ﴿by those that spread widely,﴾ ﴿by those that separate decisively,﴾ ﴿by those that deliver a reminder,﴾ ﴿as an excuse or a warning﴾. In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that these five words either refer to one single category or to several different categories.

As for the first possibility, they have mentioned several views on it.

The first: all of them refer to the angels. So "those sent forth" are the angels whom God sent, either to deliver blessing to some people or to deliver punishment to others.

As for His saying ﴿'urfan (in succession)﴾, it has several meanings:
One of them: successive, like the hair of the mane (ʿurf), as it is said: "They came as one mane," and "they gathered against him like the mane of the hyena" when they massed together against him.
The second: that it means ʿurf (customary goodness), which is the opposite of denial (nukra). For if these angels were sent for mercy, this meaning is evident in them; and if they were sent for punishment, that punishment, although it may not be known to the disbelievers, is known to the prophets and believers for whom God took vengeance upon them.
The third: that it is a verbal noun, as if it were said: "by those sent forth with sending," meaning in succession. The accusative of ﴿'urfan﴾ according to the first meaning is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl); according to the second, it is an object, meaning: they were sent for goodness and customary kindness.

As for His saying ﴿fa-l-ʿāṣifāti ʿaṣfan (and by those that blow with violent blowing)﴾, it has two meanings:
The first: that when God the Exalted sent those angels, they swept through in their flight just as winds sweep.
The second: that these angels sweep away the soul of the disbeliever. It is said: "he swept away the thing" when he destroyed it and annihilated it. It is said: "a she-camel that sweeps (ʿaṣūd)," meaning she sweeps her rider away and passes on as if she were a wind in speed; and "war swept the people away," meaning it carried them off. The poet said:

*In a host, white and massed, it sweeps away the one who advances and the one who retreats.*

[Page 234]

As for His exalted saying ﴿wa-n-nāshirāti nashran (and by those that spread widely)﴾, its meaning is that they spread their wings when they descend to the earth; or they spread the laws upon the earth; or they spread mercy or punishment; or the intended meaning is the angels who spread the books on the Day of Reckoning, which are the books containing the deeds of the children of Adam. God the Exalted said: ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find spread open﴾ [al-Isra: 13]. In sum, they have spread the thing they were commanded to deliver to the people of the earth and to spread among them.

As for His exalted saying ﴿fa-l-fāriqāti farqan (and by those that separate decisively)﴾, its meaning is that they distinguish between truth and falsehood.

As for His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾, its meaning is that they deliver the reminder to the prophets. Then the meaning of "reminder" may be the general knowledge and wisdom, as He said: ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [al-Nahl: 2]. It may also be that the intended meaning is the Qur'an specifically, as in His saying: ﴿Has the reminder been cast upon him from among us?﴾ [al-Qamar: 25], and His saying: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be cast to you﴾ [al-Qasas: 86]. And although this one who casts it is Jibril alone, peace be upon him, it is permissible to refer to one by the name of a group as a form of honour.

Know that you have already understood that the purpose of an oath is to draw attention to the greatness of what is sworn by. The nobility of the angels and the loftiness of their rank is evident from several aspects:

One of them: the intensity of their constancy in obeying God the Exalted, as He said: ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾, and ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya: 27].

The second: they are of various categories. Among them are those sent to bring down revelation to the prophets; among them are those sent to accompany the children of Adam to record their deeds, a group by day and a group by night; among them are those sent to seize the souls of the children of Adam; among them are those who convey revelation from one heaven to another until the angel of that heaven brings the revelation down to the earth; and among them are the angels who descend every day from the Bayt al-Ma'mur to the Ka'ba, as has been reported in the traditions. All of this is included in His saying: ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾. Then there is the swiftness of their movement and their crossing of great distances in a short time, as in His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 4]. Then there is the spreading of their great wings when they fly, and the spreading of knowledge, wisdom, prophethood, guidance, direction, revelation and sending down, and the manifestation of the distinction between truth and falsehood through the sending down of that revelation, and the casting of the reminder into the heart and tongue through that revelation. In sum, the angels are the intermediaries between God the Exalted and His servants in attaining all worldly and otherworldly felicities, and both bodily and spiritual goods. Therefore God swore by them.

The second view: the intended meaning of all these five words is the winds. God swore by winds of punishment which He sent "in succession," meaning successive like the hair of the mane, as He said: ﴿He sends the winds﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], and ﴿And We sent the winds﴾ [al-Hijr: 22]. Then they grow strong until they become violent storms, and winds of mercy, which spread the clouds across the sky, as He said: ﴿And He it is who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], and He said: ﴿God is the One who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and He spreads them across the sky﴾ [al-Rum: 48]. It is also permissible to say that the winds assist plants, crops and trees in growth and sprouting, because they fertilise them, and thereby the plants emerge. This is as He said: ﴿And We sent the fertilising winds﴾ [al-Hijr: 22]. In this way the winds are spreaders of plant life. As for the winds being separators, there are several aspects:

One of them: the winds separate some parts of the clouds from others.

The second: God the Exalted destroyed some towns by sending winds upon them, as He said: ﴿As for ʿĀd, they were destroyed by a violent screaming wind﴾ [al-Haqqa: 6], and that is a cause for the manifestation of the distinction between the friends of God and His enemies.

The third: when various winds arise and wondrous effects follow from them, such as the surging of clouds and the ruin of dwellings, people become compelled to return to God

[Page 235]

and to humble themselves at the door of His mercy. Thus a distinction arises between the one who affirms and the one who denies, and between the monotheist and the heretic. As for His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾, its meaning is that when a rational person witnesses the blowing of winds that uproot tents, demolish rocks and mountains, and raise waves, he holds fast to the remembrance of God and takes refuge in the help of God. So those winds become as if they had cast the remembrance, faith and servitude into the heart. There is no doubt that this attribution is figurative, since the remembrance came about at the occurrence of these winds.

The third view: some people have taken some of these five words to refer to the Qur'an, and in my opinion it is possible to take all of them as referring to the Qur'an. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth﴾ means the consecutive verses sent down through Jibril, peace be upon him, to Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying ﴿in succession﴾ means that these verses came down with every kind of customary goodness and benefit, and how could they not, since they guide to the path of salvation and lead to the gathering of all good. ﴿By those that blow with violent blowing﴾ means that the state of Islam and the Qur'an was weak at first, then it grew great and overcame all other religions, communities and creeds. It is as if the state of the Qur'an swept away all other states, communities and creeds, overpowered them, and made them false and void. His saying ﴿by those that spread widely﴾ means that the verses of the Qur'an spread the effects of wisdom and guidance into the hearts of the worlds, east and west. His saying ﴿by those that separate decisively﴾ is evident, because the verses of the Qur'an are what distinguish truth from falsehood, and for this reason God the Exalted named the Qur'an "the Criterion" (al-furqan). His saying ﴿by those that deliver a reminder﴾ is also clear, because the Qur'an is a reminder, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Ṣād. By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾, ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾, and "admonition" (tadhkira), as He said: ﴿And indeed it is an admonition for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Haqqa: 48], and "remembrance" (dhikra), as He said: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder for the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. It thus becomes clear that these five words can be interpreted as referring to the Qur'an. Although no one has mentioned this, it is still a possibility.

The fourth view: these words may also be taken to refer to the sending of the prophets, peace be upon them all. ﴿By those sent forth in succession﴾ are the persons who were sent with revelation containing every good and customary goodness, for there is no doubt that they were sent with "There is no god but God," which is the key to all good and customary goodness. ﴿By those that blow with violent blowing﴾ means that the affair of each messenger is at first small and weak, then it grows, becomes great, and gains strength like the blowing of winds. ﴿By those that spread widely﴾ means the spreading of their religion, their way and their doctrine. ﴿By those that separate decisively﴾ means that they distinguish between truth and falsehood, monotheism and atheism. ﴿By those that deliver a reminder﴾ means that they call creation to the remembrance of God, command them to it, and urge them towards it.

The fifth view: the intended meaning is that a man may be occupied with the interests of this world, absorbed in seeking its pleasures and comforts. In the midst of that, there arises in his heart a call to turn away from this world and to desire the service of his Master. These callings are "those sent forth in succession." These sent callings have two effects:

One of them: the removal of love for anything other than God the Exalted from the heart. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿by those that blow with violent blowing﴾.

The second: the effect of that call becomes manifest in all the limbs and organs, so that he hears only God, sees only God, and looks only to God. This is His saying ﴿by those that spread widely﴾. Then at that point the light of God's majesty is unveiled to him, so he sees Him as existent and sees everything else as non-existent. This is His saying ﴿by those that separate decisively﴾. Then the servant becomes like one who is famed for his love, and nothing remains in his heart or on his tongue except the remembrance of Him. This is His saying ﴿by those that deliver a reminder﴾.

Know that these last three aspects, although they have not been mentioned, are very much possible.

As for the second possibility, which is that the five words do not refer to one single thing, there are several views:

The first: what al-Zajjaj mentioned and what al-Qadi chose, namely that the first three are winds. So His saying ﴿by those sent forth in succession﴾ refers to the winds that come in the customary manner, "those that blow with violent blowing" refers to the winds that intensify from it, and "those that spread widely" refers to the winds that spread the clouds.

[Page 236]

As for His saying ﴿fa-l-fāriqāti farqan (and by those that separate decisively)﴾, these are the angels who distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful, through what they bear of the Qur'an and revelation. Likewise His saying ﴿fa-l-mulqiyāti dhikran (and by those that deliver a reminder)﴾ refers to the angels who bear the reminder and deliver it to the messengers.

The Exalted said: "Indeed, what you are promised is surely going to occur" (Qur'an 77:7). This is the answer to the oath, and the meaning is: that which you are promised of the coming of the Day of Resurrection is certainly going to take place and descend. Al-Kalbi said: the intended meaning is that everything you are promised, of good and of evil, is certainly going to occur. Those who held the first interpretation argued that after these verses God mentioned the signs of the Day of Resurrection, which indicates that what is intended by this verse is the Resurrection alone; then He mentioned the signs of the occurrence of this Day.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 77, verses 8–14:**

The first point: His saying, ﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾. We have already discussed the meaning of *tams* (obliteration) at His saying, ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth﴾ [Yunus: 88]. In general, it may mean that their essences are annihilated, which agrees with His saying, ﴿when the stars fall﴾ and ﴿when the stars lose their light﴾. It may also mean that their lights are annihilated. The first is preferable, because it does not require an implied element. It is also possible that their light is obliterated and then they fall while their light is extinguished.

The second point: His saying, ﴿And when the sky is split open﴾. *Al-farj* means a cleft (*al-shaqq*). It is said: "He split it, and it split open," and every cleft is a *farj*. Here, His saying "*fururijat*" means "*shuqqat*" (was cleaved). A parallel is ﴿When the sky is rent asunder﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 1] and ﴿The day the sky will split open with clouds﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. Ibn Qutaybah said: its meaning is "*futihat*" (was opened). A parallel is ﴿And the sky is opened﴾. The poet said:

*The one who opens the gate of the obscure prince*

The third point: His saying, ﴿And when the mountains are blown away﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: they are blown away like grain that has been winnowed when it is sifted with a winnowing shovel. From this is His saying, ﴿Then we will burn it and then we will scatter it [into the sea]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 97]. A parallel is ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5], ﴿and the mountains will become heaps of sand poured out﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14], and ﴿Say: My Lord will scatter them as dust﴾ [Ta-Ha: 105].

The second: they are uprooted swiftly from their places, from *intasaftu al-shay'* when you snatch the thing away quickly. It has been read as "*tumissat*," "*furrijat*," and "*nussifat*" with a doubled letter (shaddah).

[Page 238]

The fourth point: His saying, ﴿And when the messengers are brought to their appointed time﴾. Regarding this there are two issues:

The first issue: "*uqqitat*" originally was "*wuqqitat*" (from *waqt*, time, with an original *waw*). Several points show this:

One: the reading of Abu 'Amr: "*wuqqitat*" with a *waw*.

Two: the root of the word is from *al-waqt* (time).

Three: every *waw* that takes a *damma* and whose *damma* is necessary is regularly changed into a *hamza*, both at the beginning and in the middle of a word. From this you say: *ṣalla al-qawmu ihdānan* (the people prayed in ihdānan), and these are fine forms, and *adwur* as the plural of *dar* (house). The reason is that the *damma* is of the same kind as the *waw*, so combining them is like combining two similar letters, which becomes heavy. For this reason, the *kasra* on the *ya'* is also heavy.

As for His saying, ﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], the change to *hamza* is not permitted there, because the *damma* is not necessary. Do you not see that it is not permissible in a phrase like your saying ﴿this promise﴾ [al-Anbiya': 38] to change it?

The second issue: regarding *al-ta'qit* (fixing the time), there are two views:

The first, which is the view of Mujahid and al-Zajjaj: it is clarifying the time at which they will be present to testify against their nations. This view is weak, because these things have been made signs of the establishment of the Resurrection. It is as if it were said: when such and such happens, the Resurrection will occur. It is not appropriate in this context to say: when He clarifies for them the time at which they will be present to testify against their nations, the Resurrection occurs. That clarification was already present in this world. Also, the three preceding things, namely the obliteration, the splitting, and the scattering, are specific to the time of the establishment of the Resurrection. Therefore this appointing of time must also be specific to the time of the establishment of the Resurrection.
