It may also mean that their lights are annihilated. The first is preferable, because it does not require an implied element. It is also possible that their light is obliterated and then they fall while their light is extinguished.

The second point: His saying, ﴿And when the sky is split open﴾. *Al-farj* means a cleft (*al-shaqq*). It is said: "He split it, and it split open," and every cleft is a *farj*. Here, His saying "*fururijat*" means "*shuqqat*" (was cleaved). A parallel is ﴿When the sky is rent asunder﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 1] and ﴿The day the sky will split open with clouds﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. Ibn Qutaybah said: its meaning is "*futihat*" (was opened). A parallel is ﴿And the sky is opened﴾. The poet said:

*The one who opens the gate of the obscure prince*

The third point: His saying, ﴿And when the mountains are blown away﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: they are blown away like grain that has been winnowed when it is sifted with a winnowing shovel. From this is His saying, ﴿Then we will burn it and then we will scatter it [into the sea]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 97]. A parallel is ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5], ﴿and the mountains will become heaps of sand poured out﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14], and ﴿Say: My Lord will scatter them as dust﴾ [Ta-Ha: 105].

The second: they are uprooted swiftly from their places, from *intasaftu al-shay'* when you snatch the thing away quickly. It has been read as "*tumissat*," "*furrijat*," and "*nussifat*" with a doubled letter (shaddah).

[Page 238]

The fourth point: His saying, ﴿And when the messengers are brought to their appointed time﴾. Regarding this there are two issues:

The first issue: "*uqqitat*" originally was "*wuqqitat*" (from *waqt*, time, with an original *waw*). Several points show this:

One: the reading of Abu 'Amr: "*wuqqitat*" with a *waw*.

Two: the root of the word is from *al-waqt* (time).

Three: every *waw* that takes a *damma* and whose *damma* is necessary is regularly changed into a *hamza*, both at the beginning and in the middle of a word. From this you say: *ṣalla al-qawmu ihdānan* (the people prayed in ihdānan), and these are fine forms, and *adwur* as the plural of *dar* (house). The reason is that the *damma* is of the same kind as the *waw*, so combining them is like combining two similar letters, which becomes heavy. For this reason, the *kasra* on the *ya'* is also heavy.

As for His saying, ﴿And do not forget graciousness among yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237], the change to *hamza* is not permitted there, because the *damma* is not necessary. Do you not see that it is not permissible in a phrase like your saying ﴿this promise﴾ [al-Anbiya': 38] to change it?

The second issue: regarding *al-ta'qit* (fixing the time), there are two views:

The first, which is the view of Mujahid and al-Zajjaj: it is clarifying the time at which they will be present to testify against their nations. This view is weak, because these things have been made signs of the establishment of the Resurrection. It is as if it were said: when such and such happens, the Resurrection will occur. It is not appropriate in this context to say: when He clarifies for them the time at which they will be present to testify against their nations, the Resurrection occurs. That clarification was already present in this world. Also, the three preceding things, namely the obliteration, the splitting, and the scattering, are specific to the time of the establishment of the Resurrection. Therefore this appointing of time must also be specific to the time of the establishment of the Resurrection.

The second view: the meaning of this appointing of time is the bringing about and creation of the time. This is also closer to the correspondence with the wording, because the pattern of the *tafʿīl* forms is based on bringing about those realities. *Al-taswid* is bringing about blackness, and *al-tahrik* is bringing about motion. Likewise *al-ta'qit* is bringing about a time. Moreover, the wording does not state whose time it is the bringing about of. It was not specified and not defined so that the mind would wander in every direction, making the awe in it greater. So it may mean the creation of the time at which they will be present to testify against their nations, or it may be the time at which they gather to win reward, or it may be the time of questioning the messengers about what they were answered with and questioning the nations about what they answered them, as He said: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6]. Or it may be the time at which they witness Paradise, Hell, the presentation, the reckoning, the weighing, and the rest of the conditions of the Resurrection. To this the verse alludes in His saying: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah, their faces blackened﴾ [al-Zumar: 60].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 77, verse 15:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿For what day has it been postponed?﴾ That is, it has been delayed. It is as if the Exalted is astonishing the servants at the magnitude of that day, so He says: For what day have the matters connected with these (messengers) been postponed? These are the punishment of those who denied them, the honouring of those who believed in them, and the manifestation of what they used to call creation to believe in, namely the terrors, the presentation (ʿarḍ), the reckoning (ḥisāb), the spreading out of the records (dawawīn), and the setting up of the scales (mawāzīn).

Then the Exalted explained that, saying: ﴿For the Day of Decision.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: It is the day on which the Merciful (al-Raḥmān) decides between the creatures. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is their appointed time, all of them.﴾ [al-Dukhān: 40]

Then He followed this with a second magnification, saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ That is: And what knowledge do you have of the Day of Decision, its severity and its awesomeness?

Then He followed it with a third terrifying description, saying: ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers.﴾ That is, to those who deny the Oneness of God, prophethood, the Return, and everything that the prophets, upon them be peace, brought and reported about. Two questions remain here:

The first question: How did the indefinite noun come to be the subject (mubtada') in His saying: ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾?
The answer: Originally it is a verbal noun in the accusative, standing in place of its verb, but it was shifted to the nominative to indicate the meaning of the permanence and continuity of destruction for the one against whom it is invoked. Similar to it is ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 55]. It is permissible to say "waylan" in the accusative, but it has not been recited with it.

The second question: Where is the answer to His saying: ﴿When the stars are extinguished﴾? The answer is from two aspects:

One of them: The estimate is: "What you are promised is surely going to occur when the stars are extinguished." This is weak, because it would occur at His saying: ﴿When the stars are extinguished.﴾

The second: The answer is omitted, and the estimate is: ﴿When the stars are extinguished﴾ and when, and when; then recompense for deeds takes place, and the Resurrection is established.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 77, verses 16–19:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾ ﴿Then We follow them with the latter.﴾ ﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals.﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾ Know that the purpose of this passage is to frighten the disbelievers and warn them against disbelief.

The first type of frightening is that He swore an oath that the Day they are promised, which is the Day of Judgment (*yawm al-fasl*), will certainly come. Then He made it terrifying, saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is?﴾ Then He increased the terror, saying: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾

The second type of frightening is what is mentioned in this verse, namely that He destroyed the disbelieving peoples of the past because of their disbelief. So if disbelief is present in these later people, then He must destroy them as well. Then He said: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾ It is as if He is saying: As for this world, their lot is destruction, and as for the Hereafter, it is severe punishment. To this refers His saying: ﴿They have lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.﴾ [al-Hajj: 11]

There are two questions regarding the verse.

The first: What is meant by "the former" and "the latter"?

The answer: There are two opinions.

The first: He destroyed the former peoples, such as the people of Noah, ʿĀd and Thamūd, and then He followed them with the latter, such as the people of Shuʿayb, Lot and Moses. ﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. This opinion is weak, because His saying ﴿We follow them﴾ is in the present tense (*al-muḍāriʿ*), which covers the present and the future and does not cover the past at all.

The second opinion: "The former" refers to all the disbelievers who lived before Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying ﴿Then We follow them with the latter﴾ is a resumed statement (*al-istiʾnaf*), meaning: We shall do that, and We shall make the first followed by the last. What supports the resumption is the recitation of ʿAbd Allah: "*sa-nutbiʿuhum*" (سَنُتْبِعُهُمُ, "We shall follow them"). If it is said: al-Aʿraj recited "*thumma nutbiʿhum*" (ثُمَّ نُتْبِعْهُمُ) with a jussive ending, and that indicates that it is linked to "*alam*" (did We not), and in that case it refers to the past and not the future, we reply: The established recitation by mass transmission (*tawātur*) is "*nutbiʿuhum*" (نُتْبِعُهُمُ) with a vowel on the ʿayn, and that requires the future. If the recitation with the jussive were to require that the meaning be the past, the two recitations would contradict each other, and that is not permissible. So we know that the sukun on the ʿayn is not for the jussive but for lightening (*al-takhfīf*), as is reported in the line of Imruʾ al-Qays:

*"And today I drink, not storing up (for tomorrow)."*

Then, when He made clear that He deals with these later people in the same way He dealt with those earlier ones, He said: ﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals.﴾ That is: This destruction is something We do to them only because they are criminals. Therefore it applies generally to all criminals, because the generality of the cause requires the generality of the ruling.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾ That is: Even though these were destroyed and punished in this world, the greatest calamity and the supreme catastrophe are prepared for them on the Day of Resurrection.

The second question: Is the destruction in His saying ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾ absolute causing of death, or death by punishment? If it is the first, it would not be a frightening for the disbelievers, because that is something that happens to both the believer and the disbeliever, so it is not suitable as a warning to the disbeliever. If the intended meaning is the second, death by punishment, then His saying ﴿Then We follow them with the latter. Thus do We deal with the criminals﴾ requires that God has done the same to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and it is known that this did not happen. Also, He said: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33].

The answer: Why should it not be possible that the intended meaning is causing death through punishment, and that this did occur with regard to Quraysh, namely at the Day of Badr? Granting that, why should it not be possible that the meaning of destruction is a third meaning, different from the two that they mentioned, namely causing death that results in blame and curse? It is as if it is said: Those earlier peoples, because of their greed for this world, opposed the prophets and disputed with them, and then they died. Thus this world escaped them, the curse remained upon them in this world, and the punishment of the Hereafter is perpetual, everlasting. So it is the same with these present disbelievers. It is known that this kind of speech is among the greatest forms of admonition.

Know that this is the third type of the warning to the disbelievers, and the warning in it has two aspects.

The Sūrah (77:25-28), Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb of al-Rāzī:

﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle,﴾ ﴿for the living and the dead?﴾ ﴿And We placed in it firm, towering mountains, and gave you sweet water to drink.﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers!﴾

Know that this is the fourth kind of warning to the disbelievers. He reminded them of the blessings He bestowed upon them within themselves, and in this verse He reminded them of the blessings He bestowed upon them in the horizons. Then He said at the end of the verse: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers!﴾ The reason for this is what we previously mentioned: the more numerous the blessings, the more hideous the offence, so the deserving of blame in this world and of punishment in the next becomes more severe. He placed that verse before this one because the blessings within the self are like the root of the blessings in the horizons, for without life, hearing, sight and sound limbs, benefiting from any of the created things would not be possible.

Know that He, may He be exalted, mentioned three things here:

The first is the earth. He mentioned it first because the nearest of external things to us is the earth. The meaning of *kifāt* (receptacle) in the language is gathering and collecting. It is said: *kafattu al-shay'* meaning I gathered the thing. It is said: a *jirāb kafīt* or *kift* when it does not lose anything placed in it. And it is said of a cooking pot: *kift*. The author of al-Kashshāf said: it is the name of that which gathers, like their saying *al-ḍimām* and *al-jimā'* for that which gathers and collects. It is said: this chapter is the *jimā'* of the chapters. You say: *shaddadtu al-shay'*, then you call the cord with which you bind the thing *shidād*. With it, *aḥyā'an wa-amwātan* is in the accusative, as if it were said: *kāfitatan aḥyā'an wa-amwātan* (gathering the living and the dead), or by a hidden verb that indicates it, which is *nakfitu*, and the meaning would be: We gather you, living and dead, and both are in the accusative as circumstantial states of the pronoun. This is the linguistic aspect. Then, regarding meaning, there are several views:

One of them: it gathers the living upon its back and the dead in its belly. The meaning is that the living dwell in their homes and the dead are buried in their graves. For this reason they used to call the earth "mother", because in its gathering of people it is like the mother who gathers her child and nurtures it. And since they are gathered into it, it was made as if it gathers them.

Second: it is a receptacle for the living, in the sense that it gathers what is discharged from the living of repulsive matters. As for it gathering the living while they are upon its back, that is not the case.

Third: it is a receptacle for the living in the sense that it contains what man needs in his necessities, of food and drink, because all of that comes out of the earth, and the buildings that gather benefits and repel harms are built from it.

Fourth: His saying *aḥyā'an wa-amwātan* means something that returns to the earth, the living being that which has been made to grow, and the dead being that which has not been made to grow.

Two questions remain regarding the verse:

The first: why was it said *aḥyā'an wa-amwātan* in the indefinite, when it is the receptacle of the living and the dead together? The answer: it is from the indefinite of magnification (*tankīr al-tafkhīm*), as if it were said: it gathers living ones who cannot be counted and dead ones who cannot be enumerated.

The second question: does this verse indicate the obligation of cutting off the hand of the grave-robber (*nabbāsh*)? The answer: al-Qaffāl transmitted that Rabī'ah said: the verse indicates that the earth is the receptacle of the dead, so it is a protected place (*ḥirz*) for them, and whoever steals from a protected place is liable to amputation.

The second kind of blessing mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿And We placed in it firm, towering mountains.﴾ *Rawāsiya* means fixed and immovable on the surface of the earth, and *shāmikhāt* means high. Everything high is *shāmikh*, and it is said of the arrogant: *shāmikh bi-anfihi* (haughty with his nose). The benefits of the creation of mountains have already been mentioned in this book.

The third kind of blessing: His saying: ﴿And gave you sweet water to drink.﴾ *Al-furāt* is the utmost in sweetness, and its interpretation has already been given in His saying: ﴿This is sweet and palatable﴾ [al-Furqān: 53].

Third: it is a receptacle for the living in the sense that it contains what man needs in his necessities, of food and drink, because all of that comes out of the earth, and the buildings that gather benefits and repel harms are built from it.

Fourth: His saying *aḥyā'an wa-amwātan* means something that returns to the earth, the living being that which has been made to grow, and the dead being that which has not been made to grow.

Two questions remain regarding the verse:

The first: why was it said *aḥyā'an wa-amwātan* in the indefinite, when it is the receptacle of the living and the dead together? The answer: it is from the indefinite of magnification (*tankīr al-tafkhīm*), as if it were said: it gathers living ones who cannot be counted and dead ones who cannot be enumerated.

The second question: does this verse indicate the obligation of cutting off the hand of the grave-robber (*nabbāsh*)? The answer: al-Qaffāl transmitted that Rabī'ah said: the verse indicates that the earth is the receptacle of the dead, so it is a protected place (*ḥirz*) for them, and whoever steals from a protected place is liable to amputation.

Everything high is *shāmikh*, and it is said of the arrogant: *shāmikh bi-anfihi* (haughty with his nose). The benefits of the creation of mountains have already been mentioned in this book.

The third kind of blessing: His saying: ﴿And gave you sweet water to drink.﴾ *Al-furāt* is the utmost in sweetness, and its interpretation has already been given in His saying: ﴿This is sweet and palatable﴾ [al-Furqān: 53].

The Sūrah (77:25-28), Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb of al-Rāzī:

﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle,﴾ ﴿for the living and the dead?﴾ ﴿And We placed in it firm, towering mountains, and gave you sweet water to drink.﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers!﴾

Know that this is the fourth kind of warning to the disbelievers. He reminded them of the blessings He bestowed upon them within themselves, and in this verse He reminded them of the blessings He bestowed upon them in the horizons. Then He said at the end of the verse: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers!﴾ The reason for this is what we previously mentioned: the more numerous the blessings, the more hideous the offence, so the deserving of blame in this world and of punishment in the next becomes more severe. He placed that verse before this one because the blessings within the self are like the root of the blessings in the horizons, for without life, hearing, sight and sound limbs, benefiting from any of the created things would not be possible.

Know that He, may He be exalted, mentioned three things here:

The first is the earth. He mentioned it first because the nearest of external things to us is the earth. The meaning of *kifāt* (receptacle) in the language is gathering and collecting. It is said: *kafattu al-shay'* meaning I gathered the thing. It is said: a *jirāb kafīt* or *kift* when it does not lose anything placed in it. And it is said of a cooking pot: *kift*. The author of al-Kashshāf said: it is the name of that which gathers, like their saying *al-ḍimām* and *al-jimā'* for that which gathers and collects. It is said: this chapter is the *jimā'* of the chapters. You say: *shaddadtu al-shay'*, then you call the cord with which you bind the thing *shidād*. With it, *aḥyā'an wa-amwātan* is in the accusative, as if it were said: *kāfitatan aḥyā'an wa-amwātan* (gathering the living and the dead), or by a hidden verb that indicates it, which is *nakfitu*, and the meaning would be: We gather you, living and dead, and both are in the accusative as circumstantial states of the pronoun. This is the linguistic aspect. Then, regarding meaning, there are several views:

One of them: it gathers the living upon its back and the dead in its belly. The meaning is that the living dwell in their homes and the dead are buried in their graves. For this reason they used to call the earth "mother", because in its gathering of people it is like the mother who gathers her child and nurtures it. And since they are gathered into it, it was made as if it gathers them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 77, verses 29–34 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Go towards that which you used to deny.﴾ ﴿Go towards a shadow of three branches,﴾ ﴿neither providing shade nor sufficing against the blaze.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it throws sparks like a fortress,﴾ ﴿as if they were yellow camels.﴾ ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers!﴾

Know that this is the fifth aspect of the ways in which the disbelievers are warned, namely the explanation of the manner of their punishment in the Hereafter. As for His saying, ﴿Go towards that which you used to deny,﴾ the meaning is that it will be said to them: ﴿Go towards that which you used to deny﴾ of the punishment. Apparently, those who say this are the guardians of the Fire (khazanat al-nar). The second "go" is a repetition. Ya'qub read "inṭalaqū" in the past tense (ʿalā lafẓ al-māḍī), and the meaning is that they submitted to the command because they were compelled to it and could not resist it. This is far-fetched, because it should have been said "fa-inṭalaqū" with the fa', so that the end of the speech would be connected to its beginning. The exegetes said: On the Day of Resurrection the sun will draw near to the heads of creation, and they will have no clothing or covering that day, so the sun will scorch them, blister them and take hold of their breaths, and that day will be prolonged. Then Allah, by His mercy, will bring whom He wills to a shade from His shade, and there they will say: ﴿So Allah has been gracious to us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾ [al-Tur: 27]. And it will be said to the deniers: ﴿Go towards that which you used to deny﴾ of the punishment and retribution of Allah.

His saying ﴿towards a shadow﴾ means the smoke of Hell, as in His saying: ﴿and a shadow of black smoke﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 43]. Then He, the Exalted, described this shadow with attributes:

The first attribute: His saying ﴿of three branches﴾, and concerning it there are several views:

First: al-Hasan said: "I do not know what this shadow is, nor have I heard anything about it."

Second: Some people said: The intended meaning of His saying, ﴿towards a shadow of three branches,﴾ is that the Fire will be above them, below their feet, and encompassing them, and calling the Fire a shadow is a metaphor in that it encompasses them from every side, as in His saying: ﴿For them there will be canopies of Fire above them and canopies beneath them﴾ [al-Zumar: 16], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55].

Third: Qatadah said: Rather, the intended meaning is the smoke, from His saying: ﴿Its enclosure has surrounded them﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]; the enclosure (surādiq) of the Fire is the smoke. Then a branch of that smoke will be on its right, another branch on its left, and a third branch above it. I say: This is not far-fetched, because anger is on his right, desire is on his left, and the Satanic power is in his brain, and the source of all the afflictions that arise from a human being in his beliefs and in his deeds is none other than these three. So from these three springs there arise kinds of darknesses. It is also possible to say: here there are three degrees, namely sense, imagination and estimation (wahm), and they prevent the spirit from being illumined by the lights of the world of holiness and purity, and each of these three levels has a specific kind of darkness.

Fourth: Some people said: This is a metaphor for the greatness of that smoke, for great smoke divides into many branches.

Fifth: Abu Muslim said: "Three branches" may also be understood in light of what is mentioned after it, namely that it is not shady, that it does not avail against the blaze, and that it throws sparks like a fortress.

The second attribute of that shadow: His saying ﴿neither shady﴾. This is a mockery of them and an allusion that their shadow is not the shadow of the believers. The meaning is that this shadow does not block the heat of the sun.

The third attribute: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿nor sufficing against the blaze.﴾ It is said: "Aghni 'anni wajhaka," meaning: move it away, because one who is independent of a thing keeps away from it, just as one in need draws near to it. The author of al-Kashshaf said: It is in the genitive position (maḥall al-jarr), i.e., "and it is not sufficient for them against the heat of the blaze in any way." Al-Qaffal said: This may have two meanings:

One: that this shadow exists only in Hell, so it does not shade them from its heat nor shield them from its flame. Allah mentioned the shadow in Surat al-Waqi'ah, saying: ﴿in scorching wind and boiling water, and a shadow of black smoke, neither cool nor generous﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 42–44]. This seems to be in Hell once they have entered it, and then He said: ﴿neither cool nor generous﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 44]. So His saying ﴿neither shady﴾ may mean "neither cool," and His saying ﴿nor sufficing against the blaze﴾ may mean "nor generous," that is, there is no refreshment to which one may resort from the flame of the Fire.

The second: that its existence occurs before they enter Hell, rather when they are held back for the reckoning and the presentation, and it will be said to them: this shadow will neither shade you from the heat of the sun nor repel the flame of the Fire.

In the verse there is a second view, which is that of Qutrub: that the blaze here is thirst. It is said: "lahiba lahaban," and a man is "lahbān" and a woman is "lahbā."

The fourth attribute: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, it throws sparks.﴾ al-Wahidi said: It is said: "sharara," "shararah," "sharr," and "shirar," and it is what flies off from the fire, scattering in every direction. Its origin is from "sharartu al-thawb" when you display and spread out a garment to the sun, and the sparks spread out scattering. Know that Allah, the Exalted, described the fire of which that shadow is the smoke as throwing great sparks, and the purpose of this is to show that that fire is extremely great. Then He, the Exalted, likened those sparks to two things:

The first: to a fortress (qaṣr). Concerning its interpretation there are two views:

One: that what is meant is the building called a fortress. Ibn 'Abbas said: He means the great palaces.

The second: that this is not what is meant. Then, on that assumption, there are several interpretations:

First: that it is the plural of "qaṣrah" with the ṣād quiescent, like "tamrah" and "tamr," and "jamrah" and "jamr." al-Mubarrad said: One piece of thick, heavy firewood is called "qaṣrah," and its plural is "qaṣr." 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abis said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about the qaṣr, and he said: It is wood that we used to store for winter, cutting it, and we used to call it the qaṣr. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Muqatil and al-Dahhak, except that they said: it is the roots of palm trees and large trees. The author of al-Kashshaf said: It was read "ka-l-qaṣar" with two fatḥahs, and it means the necks of camels or the trunks of palm trees, like "shajarah" and "shajar." Ibn Mas'ud read "ka-l-quṣur" in the sense of qaṣr, like "rahn" and "ruhun." Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "ka-l-qiṣar," the plural of "qaṣrah," like "ḥājah" and "ḥiwaj."

The second comparison: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿as if they were yellow camels﴾, and in it there are two issues:

First issue: "Jimālāt" is the plural of "jimāl," as in their saying: "rijālāt" and "rijāl," and "buyūtāt" and "buyūt." Ibn 'Abbas read "jumālāt" with a ḍammah on the jīm, and this is the reading of Ya'qub. They mentioned several views:

One: It was said: "al-jumālāt" with a ḍammah means thick ropes, which are the ropes of ships, and they are called "qulūs." Some denied this and said: what is known for ropes is rather "al-jummal" with a ḍammah on the jīm and a shaddah on the mīm, and it was read: "ḥattā yalija al-jummal" [7:40].

Second: It was said: they are pieces of copper, and this is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, and Ibn 'Abbas, but most lexicographers do not know it.

Third: al-Farra' said: It is possible that "al-jumālāt" with a ḍammah is from the word "mujmal" [gathered]; one says: "ajmaltu al-ḥisāb" and "jā'a al-qawm jumlah," that is, gathered together. The meaning is that this spark rises as if it were a gathered, thick, yellow thing. This is the view of al-Farra'.

Fourth: al-Farra' said: It is possible to say "jumālāt" with a ḍammah, the plural of "jumāl" with a ḍammah, and "jumāl" with a ḍammah may be the plural of "jamal," as one says "rikhl," "rukhāl" and "rikhāl."

The second reading: "jimālah" with a kasrah on the jīm, which is the plural of "jamal," like "ḥajar" and "ḥijārah." Abu 'Ali said: The tā' was attached to "jimāl" only to indicate the feminine plural, as it was attached in "faḥl" and "fiḥālah."

The fourth reading: "jumlah" with a ḍammah on the jīm, which is the cable (al-qalas). It was also said that "ṣufr" [yellow] is meant to express the genus.

As for His saying "ṣufr," most of them hold that what is meant by it is black tending toward yellow. al-Farra' said: You do not see a black camel except that it is mixed with yellowness, and when sparks fly off and fall while still having some of the colour of fire, they resemble the black camel that has some yellowness mixed in. Some scholars claimed that what is meant is yellowness, not blackness, because a spark is called a spark only as long as it is fire, and when it is fire it is yellow; it only becomes black when it is extinguished, and then it is no longer called a spark. This view, in my opinion, is the correct one.

The second issue: Know that Allah, the Exalted, likened the sparks in greatness to a fortress, and in colour, number, succession and speed of movement to the yellow camels. It was also said that the beginning of the spark is large, so it is like a fortress, then it separates, and those scattered, successive pieces are like the yellow camels. Know that it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said, in interpreting His saying, ﴿Indeed, it throws sparks like a fortress﴾: this comparison came in the lands of the Arabs, whose palaces were low-roofed, like tents. So Allah, the Exalted, made clear that it throws sparks like a fortress. When Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri heard this, he modified it and compared it to a tent of leather, in his saying:

Red, its tresses shining in the darkness, it throws every spark like a leathern tent (ṭirāf).

Then the author of al-Kashshaf claimed that he mentioned that in opposition to this verse. I say: It would have been better for the author of al-Kashshaf not to mention that, and since he has mentioned it, we must clarify the discussion about it. We say: The comparison of the spark to a ṭirāf indicates a resemblance in shape and size. As for shape, it is from two aspects:

The first: that before it branches, the spark is like a dot of fire; when it branches it expands, so it is like a dot that expands, and it resembles a tent, for its top is like a dot, then it keeps expanding little by little.

The second: that the spark is like a sphere or a cylinder, so it is very similar to a round tent. As for the comparison to a tent in its arrangement, the matter is obvious. This is the extent of this comparison. As for the aspects in which it is faulted, they are of several kinds:

The first: that the colour of the spark is yellow mixed with some blackness, and this meaning is present in the yellow camels, and is not present in the leather tent.

The second: that camels are moving, and a tent is not moving, so comparing moving sparks with moving camels is more appropriate.

The third: that the sparks follow one another in succession, one after another, and this meaning is present in the yellow camels, and is not present in the ṭirāf.

The fourth: that the fortress is the safe refuge of a man and the place of his security, so comparing the spark to a fortress is an alert that its calamity arises from the very place where he expected safety and security, and the state of the unbeliever is like this, for he expected good and safety from his religion, then no calamity or trial appeared to him except from that religion. A leather tent is not something from which complete security is expected.

The fifth: that the Arabs used to believe that all beauty lies in possessing camels, and the perfection of blessings is attained only by owning livestock; for this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home at evening and when you send them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6]. So comparing the sparks to black camels is like a mockery of them, as if it were said to them: you used to expect from your religion honour, blessing and beauty, but that beauty is these sparks, which are like camels. This meaning is not present in the ṭirāf.

The sixth: that when camels are isolated and some of them mix with others, whoever falls among their front and hind legs at that time suffers severe affliction and great pain, so comparing the sparks to them while they follow one another conveys the attainment of complete harm, and the ṭirāf is not like that.

Page 246

**Seventh:** Apparently the *qasr* (castle) is greater in size than the *tiraf* (a kind of tent or pavilion), and the yellow camels are greater in number than the *tiraf*. So likening these sparks to the *qasr* and to the camels implies greater size and greater number. Likening them to the *tiraf* conveys neither of these. Since the aim is to inspire awe and fear, the first comparison is preferable.

**Eighth:** Likening something to two things in establishing two attributes is stronger in confirming those two attributes than likening it to one thing in establishing them. The explanation is that whoever hears His saying, ﴿Indeed it throws up sparks like a castle﴾, will immediately understand that the intent is to establish the great size of those sparks. Then, when he hears His saying after that, ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾, his mind immediately understands that the intent is the abundance of those sparks, their succession, and their color. But whoever hears that the sparks are like the *tiraf* remains uncertain whether the intended point of the comparison is establishing size or establishing color. So the comparison to the *tiraf* is like a summary (*ijmal*), while the comparison to the castle and to the yellow camels is like a detailed, repeated, and emphatic explanation. Since the purpose of this explanation is to inspire awe and fear, the more complete and clear the description of the forms of punishment, the greater the fear. Thus it is established that this comparison is more complete.

**Ninth:** He said at the beginning of the verse, ﴿Depart toward a shadow﴾. A person is only at ease while traveling and going when he is riding, and he only finds pleasant shade when he is in his castle. So the comparison of the spark to the castle and the camels is as if it were said to them: your mount is these camels, and your shade is in a castle like this. This is in the manner of mockery toward them, and this meaning is not present in the *tiraf*.

**Tenth:** It is known that a castle flying up into the air is more astonishing than a tent flying up, because a castle is built of mud brick, stone, and wood. These materials are heavier and more compact than a tent made either of cotton cloth (*kirbas*) or of leather. Whatever is heavier and more compact, its flight through the air is farther. So the fire that lifts a castle into the air is stronger than the fire that lifts a *tiraf* into the air. It is known that the aim is to magnify the matter of the fire in intensity and power, so the comparison to the castle is preferable.

**Eleventh:** The falling of a castle upon a person is more painful and more agonizing than the falling of a *tiraf* upon him. So the likening of those sparks to a castle indicates that when those sparks rise into the air and then fall upon the disbeliever, they cause him severe pain. This serves as an alert that there will not cease to fall upon him from the air sparks like castles, unlike the falling of a *tiraf* on a person, which in the end does not cause pain.

**Twelfth:** Camels are, in most matters, loaded with burdens. So the likening of the sparks to camels is an alert that with each one of those sparks there are kinds of trial and affliction whose number none but God can count. It is as if it were said: those sparks are like camels laden with kinds of trial and affliction. This meaning is not present in the *tiraf*, so the comparison to the camels is more complete.

Know that these aspects came to mind in a single instant. Had we humbly petitioned God Most High to seek more, He would have given us whatever amount we wished by His bounty and mercy. But these aspects suffice to show the preference, and adding to them would count as excessive elaboration (*itnab*). And God knows best.

And it will be said to the deniers: ﴿Go towards that which you used to deny﴾ of the punishment and retribution of Allah.

His saying ﴿towards a shadow﴾ means the smoke of Hell, as in His saying: ﴿and a shadow of black smoke﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 43]. Then He, the Exalted, described this shadow with attributes:

The first attribute: His saying ﴿of three branches﴾, and concerning it there are several views:

First: al-Hasan said: "I do not know what this shadow is, nor have I heard anything about it."

Second: Some people said: The intended meaning of His saying, ﴿towards a shadow of three branches,﴾ is that the Fire will be above them, below their feet, and encompassing them, and calling the Fire a shadow is a metaphor in that it encompasses them from every side, as in His saying: ﴿For them there will be canopies of Fire above them and canopies beneath them﴾ [al-Zumar: 16], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55].

Third: Qatadah said: Rather, the intended meaning is the smoke, from His saying: ﴿Its enclosure has surrounded them﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]; the enclosure (surādiq) of the Fire is the smoke. Then a branch of that smoke will be on its right, another branch on its left, and a third branch above it. I say: This is not far-fetched, because anger is on his right, desire is on his left, and the Satanic power is in his brain, and the source of all the afflictions that arise from a human being in his beliefs and in his deeds is none other than these three. So from these three springs there arise kinds of darknesses. Fourth: Some people said: This is a metaphor for the greatness of that smoke, for great smoke divides into many branches.

Fifth: Abu Muslim said: "Three branches" may also be understood in light of what is mentioned after it, namely that it is not shady, that it does not avail against the blaze, and that it throws sparks like a fortress.

The second attribute of that shadow: His saying ﴿neither shady﴾. This is a mockery of them and an allusion that their shadow is not the shadow of the believers. The meaning is that this shadow does not block the heat of the sun.

This seems to be in Hell once they have entered it, and then He said: ﴿neither cool nor generous﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 44]. Know that Allah, the Exalted, described the fire of which that shadow is the smoke as throwing great sparks, and the purpose of this is to show that that fire is extremely great. Then He, the Exalted, likened those sparks to two things:

The first: to a fortress (qaṣr). Concerning its interpretation there are two views:

One: that what is meant is the building called a fortress. Ibn 'Abbas said: He means the great palaces.

The second: that this is not what is meant. Then, on that assumption, there are several interpretations:

First: that it is the plural of "qaṣrah" with the ṣād quiescent, like "tamrah" and "tamr," and "jamrah" and "jamr." al-Mubarrad said: One piece of thick, heavy firewood is called "qaṣrah," and its plural is "qaṣr." The author of al-Kashshaf said: It was read "ka-l-qaṣar" with two fatḥahs, and it means the necks of camels or the trunks of palm trees, like "shajarah" and "shajar." Second: It was said: they are pieces of copper, and this is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, and Ibn 'Abbas, but most lexicographers do not know it.

Third: al-Farra' said: It is possible that "al-jumālāt" with a ḍammah is from the word "mujmal" [gathered]; one says: "ajmaltu al-ḥisāb" and "jā'a al-qawm jumlah," that is, gathered together. The meaning is that this spark rises as if it were a gathered, thick, yellow thing. This is the view of al-Farra'.

Fourth: al-Farra' said: It is possible to say "jumālāt" with a ḍammah, the plural of "jumāl" with a ḍammah, and "jumāl" with a ḍammah may be the plural of "jamal," as one says "rikhl," "rukhāl" and "rikhāl."

The second reading: "jimālah" with a kasrah on the jīm, which is the plural of "jamal," like "ḥajar" and "ḥijārah." Abu 'Ali said: The tā' was attached to "jimāl" only to indicate the feminine plural, as it was attached in "faḥl" and "fiḥālah."

The second issue: Know that Allah, the Exalted, likened the sparks in greatness to a fortress, and in colour, number, succession and speed of movement to the yellow camels. The first: that before it branches, the spark is like a dot of fire; when it branches it expands, so it is like a dot that expands, and it resembles a tent, for its top is like a dot, then it keeps expanding little by little.

The second: that the spark is like a sphere or a cylinder, so it is very similar to a round tent. As for the comparison to a tent in its arrangement, the matter is obvious. This is the extent of this comparison. As for the aspects in which it is faulted, they are of several kinds:

The first: that the colour of the spark is yellow mixed with some blackness, and this meaning is present in the yellow camels, and is not present in the leather tent.

The second: that camels are moving, and a tent is not moving, so comparing moving sparks with moving camels is more appropriate.

The third: that the sparks follow one another in succession, one after another, and this meaning is present in the yellow camels, and is not present in the ṭirāf.

The fourth: that the fortress is the safe refuge of a man and the place of his security, so comparing the spark to a fortress is an alert that its calamity arises from the very place where he expected safety and security, and the state of the unbeliever is like this, for he expected good and safety from his religion, then no calamity or trial appeared to him except from that religion. A leather tent is not something from which complete security is expected.

The fifth: that the Arabs used to believe that all beauty lies in possessing camels, and the perfection of blessings is attained only by owning livestock; for this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home at evening and when you send them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6]. So comparing the sparks to black camels is like a mockery of them, as if it were said to them: you used to expect from your religion honour, blessing and beauty, but that beauty is these sparks, which are like camels. This meaning is not present in the ṭirāf.

The sixth: that when camels are isolated and some of them mix with others, whoever falls among their front and hind legs at that time suffers severe affliction and great pain, so comparing the sparks to them while they follow one another conveys the attainment of complete harm, and the ṭirāf is not like that.

Page 246

**Seventh:** Apparently the *qasr* (castle) is greater in size than the *tiraf* (a kind of tent or pavilion), and the yellow camels are greater in number than the *tiraf*. So likening these sparks to the *qasr* and to the camels implies greater size and greater number. Likening them to the *tiraf* conveys neither of these. Since the aim is to inspire awe and fear, the first comparison is preferable.

**Eighth:** Likening something to two things in establishing two attributes is stronger in confirming those two attributes than likening it to one thing in establishing them. The explanation is that whoever hears His saying, ﴿Indeed it throws up sparks like a castle﴾, will immediately understand that the intent is to establish the great size of those sparks. Then, when he hears His saying after that, ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾, his mind immediately understands that the intent is the abundance of those sparks, their succession, and their color. But whoever hears that the sparks are like the *tiraf* remains uncertain whether the intended point of the comparison is establishing size or establishing color. So the comparison to the *tiraf* is like a summary (*ijmal*), while the comparison to the castle and to the yellow camels is like a detailed, repeated, and emphatic explanation. Since the purpose of this explanation is to inspire awe and fear, the more complete and clear the description of the forms of punishment, the greater the fear. Thus it is established that this comparison is more complete.

**Ninth:** He said at the beginning of the verse, ﴿Depart toward a shadow﴾. A person is only at ease while traveling and going when he is riding, and he only finds pleasant shade when he is in his castle. So the comparison of the spark to the castle and the camels is as if it were said to them: your mount is these camels, and your shade is in a castle like this. This is in the manner of mockery toward them, and this meaning is not present in the *tiraf*.

**Tenth:** It is known that a castle flying up into the air is more astonishing than a tent flying up, because a castle is built of mud brick, stone, and wood. These materials are heavier and more compact than a tent made either of cotton cloth (*kirbas*) or of leather. Whatever is heavier and more compact, its flight through the air is farther. So the fire that lifts a castle into the air is stronger than the fire that lifts a *tiraf* into the air. It is known that the aim is to magnify the matter of the fire in intensity and power, so the comparison to the castle is preferable.

**Eleventh:** The falling of a castle upon a person is more painful and more agonizing than the falling of a *tiraf* upon him. So the likening of those sparks to a castle indicates that when those sparks rise into the air and then fall upon the disbeliever, they cause him severe pain. This serves as an alert that there will not cease to fall upon him from the air sparks like castles, unlike the falling of a *tiraf* on a person, which in the end does not cause pain.

**Twelfth:** Camels are, in most matters, loaded with burdens. So the likening of the sparks to camels is an alert that with each one of those sparks there are kinds of trial and affliction whose number none but God can count. It is as if it were said: those sparks are like camels laden with kinds of trial and affliction. This meaning is not present in the *tiraf*, so the comparison to the camels is more complete.

Know that these aspects came to mind in a single instant. Had we humbly petitioned God Most High to seek more, He would have given us whatever amount we wished by His bounty and mercy. But these aspects suffice to show the preference, and adding to them would count as excessive elaboration (*itnab*). And God knows best.

The second: that the spark is like a sphere or a cylinder, so it is very similar to a round tent. As for the comparison to a tent in its arrangement, the matter is obvious. This is the extent of this comparison. As for the aspects in which it is faulted, they are of several kinds:

The first: that the colour of the spark is yellow mixed with some blackness, and this meaning is present in the yellow camels, and is not present in the leather tent.

The second: that camels are moving, and a tent is not moving, so comparing moving sparks with moving camels is more appropriate.

The third: that the sparks follow one another in succession, one after another, and this meaning is present in the yellow camels, and is not present in the ṭirāf.

The fourth: that the fortress is the safe refuge of a man and the place of his security, so comparing the spark to a fortress is an alert that its calamity arises from the very place where he expected safety and security, and the state of the unbeliever is like this, for he expected good and safety from his religion, then no calamity or trial appeared to him except from that religion. A leather tent is not something from which complete security is expected.

The fifth: that the Arabs used to believe that all beauty lies in possessing camels, and the perfection of blessings is attained only by owning livestock; for this reason Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home at evening and when you send them out to pasture﴾ [al-Nahl: 6]. So comparing the sparks to black camels is like a mockery of them, as if it were said to them: you used to expect from your religion honour, blessing and beauty, but that beauty is these sparks, which are like camels. This meaning is not present in the ṭirāf.

The sixth: that when camels are isolated and some of them mix with others, whoever falls among their front and hind legs at that time suffers severe affliction and great pain, so comparing the sparks to them while they follow one another conveys the attainment of complete harm, and the ṭirāf is not like that.

**Seventh:** Apparently the *qasr* (castle) is greater in size than the *tiraf* (a kind of tent or pavilion), and the yellow camels are greater in number than the *tiraf*. So likening these sparks to the *qasr* and to the camels implies greater size and greater number. Likening them to the *tiraf* conveys neither of these. Since the aim is to inspire awe and fear, the first comparison is preferable.

**Eighth:** Likening something to two things in establishing two attributes is stronger in confirming those two attributes than likening it to one thing in establishing them. The explanation is that whoever hears His saying, ﴿Indeed it throws up sparks like a castle﴾, will immediately understand that the intent is to establish the great size of those sparks. Then, when he hears His saying after that, ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾, his mind immediately understands that the intent is the abundance of those sparks, their succession, and their color. But whoever hears that the sparks are like the *tiraf* remains uncertain whether the intended point of the comparison is establishing size or establishing color. So the comparison to the *tiraf* is like a summary (*ijmal*), while the comparison to the castle and to the yellow camels is like a detailed, repeated, and emphatic explanation. Since the purpose of this explanation is to inspire awe and fear, the more complete and clear the description of the forms of punishment, the greater the fear. Thus it is established that this comparison is more complete.

**Ninth:** He said at the beginning of the verse, ﴿Depart toward a shadow﴾. A person is only at ease while traveling and going when he is riding, and he only finds pleasant shade when he is in his castle. This is in the manner of mockery toward them, and this meaning is not present in the *tiraf*.

So the fire that lifts a castle into the air is stronger than the fire that lifts a *tiraf* into the air. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 77, verses 29–34 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Go towards that which you used to deny.﴾ ﴿Go towards a shadow of three branches,﴾ ﴿neither providing shade nor sufficing against the blaze.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it throws sparks like a fortress,﴾ ﴿as if they were yellow camels.﴾ ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers!﴾

Know that this is the fifth aspect of the ways in which the disbelievers are warned, namely the explanation of the manner of their punishment in the Hereafter. As for His saying, ﴿Go towards that which you used to deny,﴾ the meaning is that it will be said to them: ﴿Go towards that which you used to deny﴾ of the punishment. Apparently, those who say this are the guardians of the Fire (khazanat al-nar). The second "go" is a repetition. Ya'qub read "inṭalaqū" in the past tense (ʿalā lafẓ al-māḍī), and the meaning is that they submitted to the command because they were compelled to it and could not resist it. This is far-fetched, because it should have been said "fa-inṭalaqū" with the fa', so that the end of the speech would be connected to its beginning. The exegetes said: On the Day of Resurrection the sun will draw near to the heads of creation, and they will have no clothing or covering that day, so the sun will scorch them, blister them and take hold of their breaths, and that day will be prolonged. Then Allah, by His mercy, will bring whom He wills to a shade from His shade, and there they will say: ﴿So Allah has been gracious to us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾ [al-Tur: 27]. And it will be said to the deniers: ﴿Go towards that which you used to deny﴾ of the punishment and retribution of Allah.

His saying ﴿towards a shadow﴾ means the smoke of Hell, as in His saying: ﴿and a shadow of black smoke﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 43]. Then He, the Exalted, described this shadow with attributes:

The first attribute: His saying ﴿of three branches﴾, and concerning it there are several views:

First: al-Hasan said: "I do not know what this shadow is, nor have I heard anything about it."

Second: Some people said: The intended meaning of His saying, ﴿towards a shadow of three branches,﴾ is that the Fire will be above them, below their feet, and encompassing them, and calling the Fire a shadow is a metaphor in that it encompasses them from every side, as in His saying: ﴿For them there will be canopies of Fire above them and canopies beneath them﴾ [al-Zumar: 16], and He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Day the punishment will cover them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55].

Third: Qatadah said: Rather, the intended meaning is the smoke, from His saying: ﴿Its enclosure has surrounded them﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]; the enclosure (surādiq) of the Fire is the smoke. Then a branch of that smoke will be on its right, another branch on its left, and a third branch above it. I say: This is not far-fetched, because anger is on his right, desire is on his left, and the Satanic power is in his brain, and the source of all the afflictions that arise from a human being in his beliefs and in his deeds is none other than these three. So from these three springs there arise kinds of darknesses. It is also possible to say: here there are three degrees, namely sense, imagination and estimation (wahm), and they prevent the spirit from being illumined by the lights of the world of holiness and purity, and each of these three levels has a specific kind of darkness.

Fourth: Some people said: This is a metaphor for the greatness of that smoke, for great smoke divides into many branches.

Fifth: Abu Muslim said: "Three branches" may also be understood in light of what is mentioned after it, namely that it is not shady, that it does not avail against the blaze, and that it throws sparks like a fortress.

The second attribute of that shadow: His saying ﴿neither shady﴾. This is a mockery of them and an allusion that their shadow is not the shadow of the believers. The meaning is that this shadow does not block the heat of the sun.

The third attribute: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿nor sufficing against the blaze.﴾ It is said: "Aghni 'anni wajhaka," meaning: move it away, because one who is independent of a thing keeps away from it, just as one in need draws near to it. The author of al-Kashshaf said: It is in the genitive position (maḥall al-jarr), i.e., "and it is not sufficient for them against the heat of the blaze in any way." Al-Qaffal said: This may have two meanings:

One: that this shadow exists only in Hell, so it does not shade them from its heat nor shield them from its flame. Allah mentioned the shadow in Surat al-Waqi'ah, saying: ﴿in scorching wind and boiling water, and a shadow of black smoke, neither cool nor generous﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 42–44]. The second: that its existence occurs before they enter Hell, rather when they are held back for the reckoning and the presentation, and it will be said to them: this shadow will neither shade you from the heat of the sun nor repel the flame of the Fire.

In the verse there is a second view, which is that of Qutrub: that the blaze here is thirst. It is said: "lahiba lahaban," and a man is "lahbān" and a woman is "lahbā."

Its origin is from "sharartu al-thawb" when you display and spread out a garment to the sun, and the sparks spread out scattering. One: that what is meant is the building called a fortress. Ibn 'Abbas said: He means the great palaces.

The second: that this is not what is meant. Then, on that assumption, there are several interpretations:

First: that it is the plural of "qaṣrah" with the ṣād quiescent, like "tamrah" and "tamr," and "jamrah" and "jamr." al-Mubarrad said: One piece of thick, heavy firewood is called "qaṣrah," and its plural is "qaṣr." One: It was said: "al-jumālāt" with a ḍammah means thick ropes, which are the ropes of ships, and they are called "qulūs." Some denied this and said: what is known for ropes is rather "al-jummal" with a ḍammah on the jīm and a shaddah on the mīm, and it was read: "ḥattā yalija al-jummal" [7:40].

Second: It was said: they are pieces of copper, and this is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, and Ibn 'Abbas, but most lexicographers do not know it.

Third: al-Farra' said: It is possible that "al-jumālāt" with a ḍammah is from the word "mujmal" [gathered]; one says: "ajmaltu al-ḥisāb" and "jā'a al-qawm jumlah," that is, gathered together. The second reading: "jimālah" with a kasrah on the jīm, which is the plural of "jamal," like "ḥajar" and "ḥijārah." Abu 'Ali said: The tā' was attached to "jimāl" only to indicate the feminine plural, as it was attached in "faḥl" and "fiḥālah."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 77, verses 35–37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is a Day on which they will not speak﴾ ﴿nor will they be permitted to offer an excuse﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾. Al-A'mash read "yawma" in the accusative, meaning: what He has related to you is occurring on that Day. Know that this is the sixth type of the ways of frightening the disbelievers and intensifying the matter upon them. This is because He, exalted is He, has made clear that they have no excuse or proof for the ugly deeds they committed, and they have no power to ward off the punishment from themselves. Thus there gather upon them in this station various kinds of punishment:

The first of them: the torment of disgrace, for he is exposed before the eyes of all witnesses, and each one's deficiency and failure becomes manifest. Anyone with sound intellect knows that the torment of disgrace is greater than being killed by the sword or burned by fire.

The second: the slave who has run away standing at the door of his master and falling into his hand, while knowing that He is the Truthful One about whom lying is impossible, as He said: ﴿The word is not changed with Me﴾ [Qaf: 29].

The third: that he sees in that station his adversaries, whom he used to look down upon and belittle, succeeding with reward and honour, while he sees himself succeeding with humiliation and punishment. These are three kinds of spiritual (rawhani) torment.

The fourth: physical torment, which is the sight of the Fire and its terrors; we seek refuge in Allah from it. When these aspects of punishment gather upon him, indeed what is beyond anything whose reality none but Allah can describe, therefore He said concerning them: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾. And in the verse there are two questions:

The first: How can one reconcile His saying: ﴿This is a Day on which they will not speak﴾ with His saying: ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord will dispute﴾ [az-Zumar: 31], and His saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], and His saying: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah a statement﴾ [an-Nisa': 42]? It is reported that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn 'Abbas about this question. The answer to it is given in several ways:

The first: al-Hasan said: there is an implied ellipsis here, and the meaning is: This is a Day on which they will not speak with a proof, nor will they be permitted to offer an excuse; because they have no sound excuse nor correct and upright answer for what they did. So when they do not speak with a sound proof and upright speech, it is as if they did not speak, for one who speaks what is not beneficial is as if he did not speak. A parallel to this is what is said to one who utters a useless statement: "You said nothing."

The second: al-Farra' said: by His saying "a Day on which they will not speak" He meant that hour and that portion of time in which they will not speak, just as one says: "I will come to you on the day that so-and-so arrives," meaning at the hour of his arrival; and the Day is not meant in its entirety, because arrival occurs in a brief hour and does not extend through the whole day.

The third: that His saying "they will not speak" is an unrestricted expression, and the unrestricted does not imply generality, neither in types nor in times, as evidenced by your saying: "So-and-so does not speak evil, but he speaks good," and at other times you say: "So-and-so does not speak at all." This shows that the concept of "does not speak" is a shared notion between not speaking some things and not speaking all things. Likewise you say: "So-and-so does not speak at this hour," and you say: "So-and-so does not speak ever." This shows that the concept of "does not speak" is common to the permanent and the temporary. When this is so, the concept of "does not speak" is satisfied by not speaking some things and at some times, and that does not contradict speaking something else at another time. Thus it suffices for the truth of His saying "they will not speak" that they do not speak with an excuse or pretext at the time of questioning. What we have mentioned indicates the soundness of the first two answers according to rational consideration. If it is said: if someone swears that he will not speak on this day, and then he speaks in a part of the day, he breaks his oath. We say: the basis of oaths is custom, whereas what we have mentioned is an investigation into the concept of the expression in itself.

The fourth: this verse came after the saying of the guardians of Hell to them: ﴿Proceed to a shadow with three branches﴾, and they comply and go. It is as if it were said: they were commanded in the world to perform acts of obedience and they did not heed; but now in this hour they have become compliant in such an obligation, which is harder than everything; as an admonition that if they had abandoned disputation in the world, they would not have needed in this hour to this arduous compliance. The sum is that His saying "This is a Day on which they will not speak" is restricted to this time and this action, and restricting the unrestricted by the context of the discourse is well-known in custom, as evidenced by the fact that if a woman says: "I will go out of the house this hour," and the husband says: "If you go out, you are divorced," this unrestricted statement is restricted to that particular going out; so it is here.

The second question: His saying "nor will they be permitted to offer an excuse" seems to imply that they have an excuse, yet they are prevented from mentioning it, and this is not befitting for the All-Wise. (The answer): In reality they have no excuse, but perhaps they imagine a corrupt fancy that they have an excuse in it, so they are not permitted to mention that corrupt excuse. Perhaps that corrupt excuse is that one says: "Since everything is by Your decree, knowledge, will, and creation, why do You punish me for it?" For this is a corrupt excuse, since no one may prevent the owner from disposing of his property however He wishes and wills. If it is said: Did He not say: ﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [an-Nisa': 165], and He said: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 134]? The purpose of all that is that no notion of having an excuse remain in his heart. Suppose his excuse on the Day of Resurrection is corrupt; then why is he not permitted to mention it until he mentions it, and then its corruption is shown to him? We say: since warning and admonition had preceded in the world, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿those who cast reminders, as an excuse or a warning﴾ [al-Mursalat: 5–6], repeating them would not be beneficial.

The third question: Why did He not say: "nor will they be permitted, so they will offer an excuse," as He said: ﴿it will not be decreed for them so that they die﴾ [Fatir: 36]? (The answer): The fa' here is merely for coordination (nasaq) and does not indicate that it is a consequent (jaza') at all. Know that this is the sixth type of the ways of frightening the disbelievers and intensifying the matter upon them. This is because He, exalted is He, has made clear that they have no excuse or proof for the ugly deeds they committed, and they have no power to ward off the punishment from themselves. Thus there gather upon them in this station various kinds of punishment:

The first of them: the torment of disgrace, for he is exposed before the eyes of all witnesses, and each one's deficiency and failure becomes manifest. Anyone with sound intellect knows that the torment of disgrace is greater than being killed by the sword or burned by fire.

The second: the slave who has run away standing at the door of his master and falling into his hand, while knowing that He is the Truthful One about whom lying is impossible, as He said: ﴿The word is not changed with Me﴾ [Qaf: 29].

The third: that he sees in that station his adversaries, whom he used to look down upon and belittle, succeeding with reward and honour, while he sees himself succeeding with humiliation and punishment. These are three kinds of spiritual (rawhani) torment.

The fourth: physical torment, which is the sight of the Fire and its terrors; we seek refuge in Allah from it. When these aspects of punishment gather upon him, indeed what is beyond anything whose reality none but Allah can describe, therefore He said concerning them: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾. And in the verse there are two questions:

The first: How can one reconcile His saying: ﴿This is a Day on which they will not speak﴾ with His saying: ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord will dispute﴾ [az-Zumar: 31], and His saying: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], and His saying: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah a statement﴾ [an-Nisa': 42]? The first: al-Hasan said: there is an implied ellipsis here, and the meaning is: This is a Day on which they will not speak with a proof, nor will they be permitted to offer an excuse; because they have no sound excuse nor correct and upright answer for what they did. So when they do not speak with a sound proof and upright speech, it is as if they did not speak, for one who speaks what is not beneficial is as if he did not speak. A parallel to this is what is said to one who utters a useless statement: "You said nothing."

The second: al-Farra' said: by His saying "a Day on which they will not speak" He meant that hour and that portion of time in which they will not speak, just as one says: "I will come to you on the day that so-and-so arrives," meaning at the hour of his arrival; and the Day is not meant in its entirety, because arrival occurs in a brief hour and does not extend through the whole day.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 77, verse 38–45:

Page 248

His words, exalted is He: ﴿This is the Day of Decision; We have gathered you and the former peoples.﴾ ﴿So if you have any scheme, then scheme against Me.﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾

Know that this is the seventh type of the threats against the disbelievers, and this part belongs to the category of punishment through reproach and humiliation. As for His saying: ﴿This is the Day of Decision﴾, know that on that Day two kinds of judgment take place:

The first: what is between the servant and the Lord. In this category, everything that relates to the Lord requires no decision, namely what relates to the reward that a person deserves for his deed. Likewise, as for punishment, a decision is needed only regarding what relates to the side of the servant, namely that their deeds which they performed be laid out before them until they confess.

The second category: what occurs between the servants themselves. This one claims against that one that he wronged him, and that one claims against this one that he killed him; here there is necessarily a decision.

His saying: ﴿We have gathered you and the former peoples﴾ is a statement clarifying His saying ﴿This is the Day of Decision﴾, because since this Day is the Day of deciding the judgments of all the accountable, it is necessary to bring together all the accountable, especially according to those who do not permit judgment in absentia. Then He said: ﴿So if you have any scheme, then scheme against Me﴾, pointing by it to the fact that they used to repel rights from themselves through various kinds of tricks and schemes. It is as if He said: here, if you are able to do such reprehensible acts of scheming, deceit, trickery and confusion, then do them. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23]. Then they know that tricks are cut off and confusions are impossible, so God's address to them in this state with His saying ﴿So if you have any scheme, then scheme against Me﴾ is the utmost in humiliation and reproach, and this is of the kind of spiritual punishment; therefore He said right after it: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing are in shades and springs﴾ ﴿and fruits of what they desire﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you used to do."﴾ ﴿Indeed, thus We reward the good-doers.﴾ ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾

Know that this is the eighth type of the threats against the disbelievers and their punishment. That is because intense enmity and great aversion existed in the world between the disbelievers and the believers, to the extent that death was easier for the disbeliever than seeing the believer possess power and dominion. When God, exalted is He, showed in this surah the gathering of the kinds of punishment, disgrace and retribution upon the disbelievers, He showed in this verse the gathering of the kinds of happiness and honor for the believer, so that the disbeliever, while seeing himself in the utmost abasement, humiliation, disgrace and loss, and seeing his opponent in the utmost might, honor, elevation and distinction, his regret doubles and his griefs and worries increase. This too is of the kind of spiritual punishment; therefore He said in this verse: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers.﴾ In the verse there are issues:

First issue: Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing﴾ are those who guard against associating partners with God. I say: this view, in my opinion, is the correct one from which there is no deviation, and several considerations indicate it:

One: whoever guards against shirk is truly called God-fearing, because the one who guards against shirk is a compound concept made of two qualifiers: first, that he is God-fearing; second, specifically that he guards against shirk. Whenever the compound exists, each of its components necessarily exists. It is thus established that everyone who is truly called one who guards against shirk is truly called God-fearing. At most one may say: on this reading the verse covers everyone who was God-fearing in any respect whatsoever. But we say: that does not undermine what we have said, because it specifies every one who was not God-fearing against all kinds of disbelief, so it remains a proof regarding what is other than that; for the general text which has entered specification remains a proof regarding what is beyond it.

Two: this surah from beginning to end is arranged to reproach the disbelievers for their disbelief and to warn them about it, so this verse must be mentioned for this purpose; otherwise the surah would fall apart in its composition and arrangement. The composition remains only if this promise is given to the believers on account of their faith; for since the threat against the disbeliever on account of his disbelief has preceded, it is necessary that this be paired with the promise to the believer on account of his faith, so that it becomes a cause for restraint from disbelief. As for pairing with it the promise to the believer on account of his obedience, that is not fitting for this composition and arrangement. Thus it is established from what we have mentioned that what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing﴾ is everyone who guards against shirk and disbelief.

Three: that carrying the wording on its complete designation is preferable, and the most complete kind of God-fearing is guarding against disbelief and shirk, so carrying the wording on it is preferable.

Second issue: when God, exalted is He, sent the disbelievers to a shade of three branches, He prepared in contrast for the believers three kinds of blessing:

The first: His saying ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing are in shades and springs﴾, as if it were said: their shades were not shady, nor did they suffice against the flame and thirst. As for the God-fearing, their shades are shady, and in them are sweet springs sufficing them against thirst and standing between them and the flame; and with them are the fruits that they desire and wish for. And when He said to the disbelievers: ﴿Go towards a shade of three branches﴾, He said to the God-fearing: ﴿Eat and drink with satisfaction﴾. Either that permission is from God, exalted is He, directly, and how great it is! Or it is from the angels in the manner of honor. The meaning of ''hanee'an'' (with satisfaction) is pure pleasure, not mixed with sickness or disturbance.

Third issue: the scholars differed as to whether His saying ﴿Eat and drink﴾ is a command or a permission. Abu Hashim said: it is a command, and God wills from them eating and drinking, because their joy is greatly increased by that; and when they know that God wills it from them as a reward for their deeds, then just as their reverence and magnification increase by that, so He wills the very eating and drinking with them. Abu 'Ali said: that is not a command; rather He means it by His saying in the manner of honor, because commands and prohibitions only take place in the time of obligation, and this is not the attribute of the Hereafter.

Fourth issue: whoever said that deeds necessitate reward took as evidence the preposition bi in His saying ﴿for what you used to do﴾. This is weak, because the bi here indicates attribution; and since God, exalted is He, made that deed a sign of this reward, performing that deed is like the instrument which leads to attaining that reward.

As for His saying ﴿Indeed, thus We reward the good-doers﴾, the purpose of it is to remind the disbelievers of the great blessings that escaped them, so that they know that had they been among the God-fearing and good-doers, they would have succeeded with the like of those goods; and since they did not do that, they inevitably fell into what they fell into.
